How to use a textbook-level course

Read one lecture, reconstruct its derivations with the text closed, and solve its examples before checking the printed calculation. Use the worksheets to consolidate a method, the practice problems to select methods independently, and the quiz to test retention. The source estimates five weeks; this expanded treatment is best paced by understanding rather than a fixed time promise.

Equations are pre-rendered from LaTeX into embedded SVG. Diagrams are original SVG with text labels and captions. Browser search finds the prose and problem statements. Use the browser’s print command for a paper or PDF copy; expand any solutions you want included before printing, since print handling of collapsed details varies by browser.

Two numbering systems are retained: five course modules and 30 lectures. The source calls lectures 2–30 “Module 2” through “Module 30”; the coverage table preserves those exact titles while the textbook uses “Lecture” to avoid ambiguity.

Complete syllabus coverage

The tables preserve the ordering of every listed video and reading, including the suspension worksheet appearing before Lecture 22 in the source. Each video maps to an original prose chapter. Each PDF reading maps to that chapter as its HTML companion. Worksheet, practice, and quiz readings map to original material. The five graded assessments are separately represented in the module files.

Scope, notation, and limits

SI units are the default. Tension is positive for truss members. Each beam, cable, or contact model declares its own directions before using signed equations. Equilibrium does not by itself establish strength, stability, or contact feasibility; the course explicitly distinguishes these tests.

The course covers the listed statics subjects with supporting derivations, examples, and a cumulative assessment. Administrative entries explain the scope of this self-study edition.

Applications of the Equations of Static Equilibrium to Interacting Bodies or Parts of a Structure; Systems Containing Multi-force Members; Frames and Machines

Lectures 1–5 · Original textbook course · Offline edition · 9 September 2026

Read the chapters in order. Work each example independently, then use the worksheets and practice set. Solutions open on demand. Repeated “continued” lecture subdivisions are editorial choices, explicitly labeled in the text.
Lecture 1

Course Introduction and Topics

Before the first equation.

A free-body diagram is a drawing of one isolated body with the forces and couples exerted on it by its surroundings. The symbol means “add all contributions.” The quantities and are signed force components along perpendicular horizontal and vertical axes. The quantity is the signed moment about the chosen point O. We take right, up, and counterclockwise as positive in planar external equilibrium. The zero on the right of an equilibrium equation means the total is zero, not that every individual force vanishes.

What this course is about

A bridge, a pair of pliers, and a suspension cable seem to demand different theories. At the level of statics, they share one question: what forces must act so that every part remains in equilibrium? The difficulty is usually not a new law of physics. It is deciding what counts as a part, which interactions cross its boundary, and which mechanical assumptions are justified. This course develops that judgment by moving from connected rigid bodies to trusses, beams, cables, and frictional contact.

An engineering model is a deliberate simplification. A steel bar is deformable, but we may treat its geometry as fixed while finding its forces. A pin has a finite diameter and some friction, but we may replace it by an ideal joint that transmits force and no couple. Neither approximation says that deformation or friction is literally absent. It says that their effects are excluded from the present model. A result is useful only if those exclusions are reasonable for the question being asked.

Throughout the course, a force is a vector and a moment measures a force's tendency to rotate a body about a point or axis. In a planar problem, the basic equations are

These equations must hold for the complete assembly and for every isolated component. Applying them only to the complete assembly often finds support reactions but hides the internal forces that matter for sizing members and joints. Applying them to carefully chosen pieces reveals those forces.

The route through the syllabus

The first module teaches the separation of assemblies into bodies. The second specializes this idea to pin-connected bars, where the unknown interaction is only an axial force. The third extends joint equilibrium into space and then introduces cuts through beams. The fourth studies flexible cables, whose geometry must accommodate tension. The fifth adds friction, where an equilibrium equation must be supplemented by an inequality describing what a contact can sustain.

There are two numbering systems in the source syllabus. Its five course modules are the five files in this course. Its lecture titles also use the word “Module,” numbered 2 through 30 after the introduction. Here those are called Lecture 2 through Lecture 30, while their exact source titles are retained in the coverage table. This prevents a lecture numbered 23 from being confused with a twenty-third course module.

A complete solution has five parts

Begin by stating the system and the assumptions. Draw a free-body diagram with all external forces and couples. Write equations using a declared coordinate system. Solve for the unknown quantities with units. Finally, test whether the result is physically admissible. A negative axial force can mean compression; a negative cable tension means that the assumed taut cable arrangement cannot exist. These are different kinds of negative answer.

Use SI units unless a problem says otherwise. A kilonewton is one thousand newtons. A moment may be reported in newton-metres or kilonewton-metres, but do not mix the two without conversion. Mass and weight are distinct: a mass of 50 kg has weight approximately 490.5 N near Earth's surface if the assumed gravitational acceleration is 9.81 metres per second squared.

Worked orientation example: a supported beam

Fig. 1.1 — External-load and support schematic. Distributed loads are replaced by their resultants only for the selected body’s equilibrium.

A weightless horizontal beam spans 4 m between a pin at A and a vertical roller reaction at B. A downward 6 kN force acts 1 m from A. The pin supplies two force components; the roller supplies one. No support supplies a couple. Taking counterclockwise moments as positive gives

Vertical equilibrium then gives , and horizontal equilibrium gives . The larger reaction belongs to the support nearer the load. This agrees with physical intuition. The reactions add to 6 kN, and the moments balance. Nothing in this calculation tells us whether the beam is strong enough; that requires its internal forces, material properties, and cross section.

If the same force moves to the midpoint, the reactions become equal. If it moves onto A, B's reaction becomes zero. Such limiting cases are inexpensive and powerful checks. A formula that fails them deserves investigation even if the algebra seems tidy.

How to study this text

Read with paper available. Before opening a solution, draw the body and predict at least one force direction. After a worked example, change one geometric parameter and predict the effect before calculating. The aim is not to recognize a diagram and retrieve a formula. It is to reconstruct the force system from the physical arrangement.

The course provides original companion readings, worksheets, and quizzes. It is aligned with the visible syllabus, not a transcription of the instructor's videos or a reproduction of the unseen official assessments. The divisions within repeated “continued” lectures are editorial choices. They develop the named subject progressively while keeping the syllabus order.

Lecture 2

Equilibrium Equations – Review from the course “Introduction to Engineering Mechanics”

Setup and symbols.

Lecture 1 introduced the isolated body; this lecture supplies its equations. Bold denotes a force vector; is a moment vector about point O. In a plane, x and y locate the force application point relative to O, while are its components. For distributed loading, is force per unit length, a and b are the loaded interval endpoints, W is the resultant load, and is its application coordinate. The integral sign means continuous summation over that interval.

Force equilibrium and moment equilibrium are independent requirements

Two equal and opposite forces can have zero resultant force and still rotate a body if their lines of action are different. Such a pair is a couple. Therefore, balancing force alone is sufficient for an ideal particle but not for a rigid body. In three dimensions, rigid-body equilibrium requires

These are six scalar equations, although geometry or constraints can make some uninformative. In a planar system, only two force components and the moment perpendicular to the plane remain. Choosing a convenient moment centre changes the algebra, not the physics. If net force is zero, a zero moment about one point implies a zero moment about every point.

Let a force act at a position whose coordinates relative to O are x and y. Its signed planar moment is

This is the perpendicular component of the cross product of the position vector with the force. It automatically uses the perpendicular distance. A common mistake is multiplying force magnitude by the distance to its application point, even when that distance is not perpendicular to the force. The cross-product expression avoids that mistake.

Replace each support by what it can transmit

A frictionless roller on a smooth surface transmits a compressive force normal to that surface. A planar ideal pin transmits two force components but no couple. A planar fixed support transmits two force components and a couple. A taut ideal cable pulls along its own direction. A two-force link supplies a force along the line joining its two interaction points. These are modeling statements; the hardware's name alone does not establish the correct idealization.

Draw only forces exerted on the isolated body. If a wall pushes on a beam, the wall's reaction belongs on the beam diagram. The beam's opposite force on the wall belongs on a different diagram. Putting both on the beam would cancel the very support interaction being modeled.

Distributed loads have a magnitude and a location

For a downward load intensity w(x), the equivalent force and its line of action are determined by

The first equation preserves total force; the second preserves moment. A uniform load acts at the midpoint of its loaded interval. A triangular load increasing from zero at the left end acts two-thirds of the interval length from that end. Its resultant equals half the peak intensity times the loaded length. This replacement is valid for external equilibrium of the selected body. It does not preserve the internal shear and moment at every point inside the loaded interval.

Worked example: oblique loading and a couple

Consider a 5 m horizontal beam pinned at A and supported by a vertical roller at B. At x = 2 m, a force has components 3 kN to the right and 4 kN downward. An additional clockwise couple of 2 kN m acts anywhere on the beam. Its position is irrelevant because a couple is a free vector for rigid-body equilibrium.

Then and . The negative horizontal result means the actual pin force acts left. Taking moments about B checks the result: the vertical force at A contributes minus 10 kN m, the downward load contributes plus 12 kN m, and the applied couple contributes minus 2 kN m. Their sum is zero.

Worked example: a triangular distribution

Fig. 1.2 — External-load and support schematic. Distributed loads are replaced by their resultants only for the selected body’s equilibrium.

A 6 m beam carries a downward load rising linearly from zero at A to 3 kN/m at B. Its resultant is 9 kN at x = 4 m. Moment equilibrium gives , so B carries 6 kN and A carries 3 kN. The reaction closer to the larger load intensity is larger, as expected. Using the midpoint for the resultant would incorrectly produce equal reactions.

Determinacy is more than counting equations

Three planar unknown reactions are not automatically solvable. Their directions must actually restrain the possible rigid-body motions. Three parallel vertical reactions do not restrain horizontal translation. Three reaction lines intersecting at one point may leave rotation unrestrained. Conversely, four reaction unknowns usually require information about deformation or support settlement in addition to statics.

Think of the equilibrium equations as a linear system. A unique solution requires enough independent equations for the unknowns. Geometric alignment can destroy independence. Later, space-truss examples will make this connection explicit through the rank of a direction matrix. For now, check both the number and the arrangement of reactions before starting a long calculation.

Why the moment origin can be changed

Proposition: moment balance is origin-independent once force balances.

Let locate force from O, and let locate another reference point Q from O. If the resultant force is zero, the total moment about Q equals the total moment about O.

Fig. 1.3 — Positions are measured from O or Q to the same force application point. Changing origin subtracts the vector OQ from every position vector.

Relative to Q, the force position is . Sum its cross product with the force and use distributivity. Applied couples, if present, enter both moment sums unchanged.

The last term vanishes only after imposing force equilibrium. Therefore a zero total moment about O also gives zero about Q. Without force equilibrium, the two moment sums can differ. This is why balancing a single moment equation is not a substitute for balancing forces.

∎

Lecture 3

2-Force Members and Multi-force Members; Introduction to Frames and Machines

Setup and symbols.

Using the equilibrium laws of Lecture 2, we now determine force directions before solving magnitudes. T denotes the assumed tensile force in a link; its horizontal and vertical components are obtained by multiplying T by the appropriate unit-vector components. are the pin forces on the bracket. A line of action is the infinite straight line through the application point parallel to the force. Concurrent forces have lines of action meeting at one point.

Why a two-force member has a known force direction

Isolate a body acted on by exactly two nonzero forces and no applied couple. Force equilibrium says that the forces are equal and opposite. Moment equilibrium about one application point says that the other force's line of action must pass through that point. The two forces must therefore be collinear. This conclusion does not require the body itself to be straight. It requires the stated loading conditions.

For a weightless link connected only by frictionless pins at A and B, the interaction direction is therefore along AB. Instead of assigning two unknown components to each end, we can describe the link with one signed axial force. If the link pulls its end joints toward one another, it is in tension. If it pushes them apart, it is in compression. A cable can supply the first action but not the second.

An apparently slender bar is not automatically a two-force member. Its own weight, a load applied at an intermediate point, or an applied couple can invalidate that classification. A straight bar with a transverse midpoint load is a multi-force member even if its ends are pinned.

Three-force bodies and concurrency

For a planar body acted on by exactly three forces and no couple, suppose two nonparallel lines of action meet at P. Their moments about P are zero. The third force must also have zero moment about P, so its line of action passes through P. The three lines are concurrent. The special alternative is that all three forces are parallel. This theorem is useful for finding an unknown reaction direction, but it must not be applied to a body with four forces or an unaccounted couple.

Worked example: a bracket held by a link

A weightless horizontal bracket AC is pinned at A = (0,0) m. A downward 8 kN force acts at C = (3,0) m. A weightless link joins D = (2,0) m on the bracket to B = (0,1.5) m on the wall. The link length is 2.5 m, so the unit vector from D toward B has components minus 0.8 and plus 0.6. Assume a tensile link force T acting on the bracket toward B.

The force at D is therefore 16 kN left and 12 kN up. Horizontal equilibrium gives . Vertical equilibrium gives , meaning the pin acts downward on the bracket. An upward link force greater than the external downward load is not a contradiction: its shorter moment arm requires it, and the pin supplies the balancing downward force.

Fig. 1.4 — Bracket free-body actions with the unloaded two-force link shown dashed for geometric reference. The solved pin vertical reaction is downward.

The bracket has three external forces: the resultant pin force at A, the link force at D, and the load at C. Their lines should be concurrent. Extend DB to x = 3 m; it meets the vertical load line at y = minus 0.75 m. The reaction at A points along the line from A to that intersection, since its vertical-to-horizontal component ratio is minus 4/16. Concurrency gives a second, geometric check on the algebra.

Why classification saves equations

If we treated the link as a general rigid body, we would introduce four endpoint components and then use equilibrium to recover their collinearity. Identifying it first builds the known physical constraint into the unknown definition. This is not a shortcut that sacrifices rigor. It is a rigorous reduction of the model.

However, it matters which body is isolated. The force the link exerts on the bracket is opposite to the force the bracket exerts on the link. On the isolated link, the force at D points down and right, while the force at B points up and left. The link is pulled outward at both ends. Keeping a sentence such as “force of link on bracket” beside an arrow can prevent a sign error that a bare label T does not reveal.

A useful distinction between structures

An ideal truss is assembled from two-force members loaded at joints. A frame supports loads and contains at least one multi-force member. A machine transmits or changes an input action into an output action and may have moving parts. In this course we analyze machines in a held configuration or under a quasi-static approximation: accelerations are neglected at the instant studied. Movement in the mechanism's possible motion does not prevent static analysis of its presently balanced forces.

The two-force theorem, with its assumptions exposed

Proposition: two nonzero endpoint forces must be equal, opposite, and collinear.

Assume a body has only forces , acting at distinct points A and B, and no applied couple.

Fig. 1.5 — The two endpoint forces on the isolated link are equal and opposite. Their shared line joins the two interaction points; the link’s outline need not follow it.

Force balance gives . Taking moments about A eliminates the force at A and gives . Because the separation is nonzero, a nonzero force must be parallel to that separation. Its line passes through B and therefore through A. The argument depends on the number of external forces, not on whether the body is straight.

If both forces vanish, equilibrium still holds but their direction is undefined. If a couple or weight is added, the premise changes and the conclusion must be re-derived.

∎

Lecture 4

Frame Structures

Setup and symbols.

Lecture 3 classified individual members. We now separate a complete frame. are support-force components acting on the frame. are defined specifically as the right member’s force on the left member at hinge C; their negatives act on the right member. A hinge transfers force but no couple. The example coordinates are in metres, and load forces are in kilonewtons.

The complete frame hides its internal forces

When two members share a pin, the forces they exert on each other cancel in the free-body diagram of the complete assembly. They do not disappear physically. They become external forces as soon as either member is isolated. This explains both the power and the limitation of whole-frame equilibrium: it finds reactions without the internal unknowns, but cannot by itself recover all member interactions.

A reliable sequence is to sketch the whole frame, identify two-force members, find any reactions obtainable globally, and then isolate a member with few unknowns. Label a shared force once and draw its opposite on the neighboring body. A frictionless internal pin transfers force but does not transfer a couple between the joined members. A rigid welded connection can transfer a couple and must be modeled differently.

Worked example: a three-hinged portal

Fig. 1.6 — Three-hinged portal geometry. The two bent members are rigid; C transfers force but no couple.

Let A = (0,0) m and B = (6,0) m be ground pins. Two rigid bent members meet at an internal hinge C = (3,3) m. A downward 12 kN load acts at D = (1,3) m on the left member. Neglect member weights. The right member has no other load, but retaining its two hinge components initially makes the action-reaction bookkeeping visible.

For the complete frame, moment equilibrium about A gives , so . Then . Horizontal equilibrium gives only ; it does not give their individual values. This is the point where the internal hinge adds useful information.

Define as the force of the right member on the left member. Vertical equilibrium of the left member gives , hence . Moments about A give

Thus and . The force on the left member at C is 2 kN left and 2 kN up. The force on the right member at C is 2 kN right and 2 kN down. For the right member, its moment about B is zero: the horizontal and vertical components each contribute 6 kN m in opposite senses. This is the independent body check that would expose an action-reaction error.

What the result means physically

The right member is actually a two-force body because only its two hinge forces act. Its resultant at C lies along CB, with slope minus one. The calculated components have precisely that direction. Its bent shape does not change the theorem. Bending stress may exist within a bent two-force body because its material does not follow the line of action, but its two external forces must still be collinear.

The horizontal support reactions are often called thrust. They arise even though the applied load is vertical. The complete assembly sees zero net horizontal force, but each component needs a horizontal interaction to balance its moment. Global symmetry is absent here because the load is not centred; nevertheless, the sum of the vertical reactions still equals the total load.

A hinge changes the available equations

If the joint at C were rigid rather than pinned, an unknown connection couple would enter the separated-body diagrams. The extra equilibrium information obtained from the zero hinge moment would be lost. With the same two ground pins, this altered structure would generally be statically indeterminate. Material stiffness and compatibility would then be needed to distribute the reactions.

A hinge does not always make a structure stable. A badly arranged set of hinges can create a mechanism. Before counting equations, imagine whether one part can move while all ideal member lengths and support constraints remain satisfied. A frame can have enough unknowns on paper and still possess an unrestrained motion.

Including member weight

To include weight, place each member's weight at its centre of gravity on that member's diagram. A previously two-force member then usually becomes a three-force or multi-force body. Do not keep its force direction constrained along the endpoint line unless the resulting geometry happens to justify it. This is a frequent modeling error when an elegant weightless solution is adapted to a real structure.

For a complicated frame, a table of joint interactions can help: one row per connection, two signed force components, and one stated body on which they act. The table is bookkeeping, not additional physics. Every numerical result should still be recoverable from a free-body diagram and equilibrium.

Lecture 5

Machine Structures

Setup and symbols.

The separated-body method from Lecture 4 also applies to a machine held in a specified configuration. P is an input-force magnitude, Q is an output-force magnitude, and a and b are their perpendicular moment arms about the pivot. In the toggle, C is each link’s compressive-force magnitude and is its angle above horizontal. The differentials dp and dq are compatible small input and output displacements, measured along the associated force directions.

Mechanical advantage is an equilibrium result

A machine can trade displacement for force. A long handle may allow a modest input force to create a large force at a nearby jaw. For an ideal lever with perpendicular input and output moment arms a and b, respectively, moment equilibrium about its pivot gives

The ratio Q/P is the force mechanical advantage for the specified force directions and configuration. It is not automatically the ratio of visible member lengths. If a force is oblique, use its perpendicular distance from the pivot or resolve its components before taking moments.

Worked example: two independently balanced handles

Consider ideal symmetric pliers with a common frictionless pivot. Each handle receives a 100 N force perpendicular to the handle, at a moment arm of 180 mm. Each jaw contacts the workpiece at a 30 mm moment arm. For one rigid handle-and-jaw member,

Each jaw therefore exerts a 600 N force on the workpiece, in opposite directions. The workpiece's net horizontal force is zero. Calling its compressive load 1200 N by adding the magnitudes would be misleading: a section through the compressed workpiece carries 600 N. If a manufacturer defines “total gripping force” as the sum of two jaw magnitudes, that is a separate reporting convention and must be stated.

To find the pivot reaction, isolate one member and balance its input and contact forces as vectors. The pivot reaction is not needed to find Q because its moment about the pivot is zero. But it matters when sizing the pin. A calculation can correctly predict output force while omitting a connection load that controls the design.

Worked example: a symmetric toggle

Fig. 1.7 — Toggle geometry and input/output forces on the surroundings. Each compressed link delivers an outward force at its guided outer end.

Two identical pin-ended links meet at a central joint. Each link makes an angle theta with the horizontal. A downward input P acts at the joint. The outer link ends lie below the centre joint and press against horizontal guides; in the ideal equilibrium the links are compressed. At the centre, their upward vertical components support P and their horizontal components cancel. Let C be the compressive magnitude in each link. Then

Here Q is the outward horizontal force at each outer end. For P = 200 N and theta = 10 degrees, C is approximately 575.9 N and Q is approximately 567.1 N. At theta = 5 degrees, Q rises to about 1143 N. The large gain near a straight configuration follows from geometry: a small vertical component requires a large axial force to balance the fixed input.

The formula tends to infinity as theta approaches zero. A real mechanism does not deliver infinite force. Elastic deformation, clearances, friction, buckling, and actuator limits become important. At exact alignment, the ideal model is singular: finite axial forces have no vertical components and cannot balance a nonzero P. The infinite limit is a warning about the idealization, not a physical prediction of unlimited capacity.

Work gives an independent explanation

For a lossless, slowly moving mechanism, input work equals output work. If two jaws each move a small distance dq against force Q while the input point moves dp under P, then

The factor two counts two outputs; it is not an arbitrary modification of the lever law. This relation is a useful check when the mechanism's geometry provides the displacement ratio. It also explains why force multiplication does not create energy: the output travels less far. This course uses direct equilibrium as the primary method, while this small-displacement viewpoint offers a second route to understanding mechanical advantage.

Machines require a configuration and an operating assumption

A diagram of a linkage without its current angles may not determine its force ratio. Likewise, a rapidly moving mechanism generally requires inertia forces and dynamic equations. Our machine examples are held in equilibrium or treated as slowly moving with negligible acceleration. If friction is present at a pin or contact, its resisting action belongs in the free-body diagram; the ideal force ratio may no longer hold.

When checking a machine solution, identify the input body, the output body, and the interaction between them. Verify each member, not only the complete machine. Internal forces may be much larger than both the input and the net external load. That amplification is often the central engineering fact the analysis is meant to discover.

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A weightless link joins (0,0) m to (3,4) m. It is tensile with force 10 kN. Find its force on the first joint. Explain what changes if the link has a downward midpoint weight.

Open a hint

Use a unit vector, then reconsider the number of external forces.

Read the full solution

The length is 5 m. Thus the force on the first joint is , directed toward the second joint. The second joint receives the opposite vector. A midpoint weight adds a third force on the link. The endpoint forces are no longer necessarily collinear with the endpoint line; treat the link as a general body and include its weight.

Read the full solution

The equation is , so T = 25 kN in tension. Its force on the bracket is (−20,15) kN. Force balance gives the pin reaction (20,−5) kN. The link pulls upward more strongly than the load because it has a shorter moment arm; the pin supplies the remaining downward force.

Open a hint

A hinge has two planar force components and no transferred couple. A weld adds an unknown interaction couple. The separated-member moment equations can no longer exploit a zero hinge moment. Practice problems

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A 4 m beam is pinned at A and has a vertical roller at B. A uniform 2 kN/m load acts over the full span, and a 4 kN force acts down at x = 1 m. Find reactions.

Replace the distribution by a resultant at its centroid.

Read the full solution

The distributed force is 8 kN at x = 2 m. Thus , giving B = 5 kN up and A = 7 kN up. There is no horizontal load, so the horizontal reaction is zero. The reactions total 12 kN.

A force (4,−3) kN acts at (2,5) m. Find its moment about the origin.

Open a hint

Use xFy minus yFx.

Read the full solution

, clockwise. The force magnitude is 5 kN, but multiplying that by the position-vector length would not give the moment because that length is not the perpendicular lever arm.

Problem 3

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A link is attached by two pins but has an applied 1 kN m couple. Is its force necessarily along the pin line?

Open a hint

Revisit every assumption of the two-force theorem.

Read the full solution

No. The couple must be balanced by endpoint forces whose lines generally have a separation. The endpoint forces still sum to zero if no other forces act, but they need not be collinear. Calling the body a two-force member would discard the applied couple.

Problem 1

A 6 m beam carries 9 kN downward at x = 2 m and a clockwise 6 kN m couple. With a left pin and right vertical roller, find reactions.

, so B = 4 kN up and A = 5 kN up. Ax = 0. Check about B: −5(6) + 9(4) − 6 = 0 kN m.

Problem 2

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A two-force link is in compression. Describe its force on each attached joint.

Read the full solution

It pushes each joint away from the opposite endpoint along the endpoint line. On the isolated link, the forces exerted by the joints point inward. These are action-reaction counterparts, not the same arrows copied to both bodies.

Problem 3

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A machine has a force ratio 8. Does an input displacement of 8 mm imply an output displacement of 1 mm?

Read the full solution

Only with the appropriate single-input/single-output, lossless, compatible small-motion assumptions and aligned work-conjugate force/displacement directions. The ratio can vary with configuration; multiple outputs require their work contributions to be included.

Extension problems: model, derive, investigate

These problems extend the foundation set. They test a conceptual distinction, a derivation, and a parameter study. The solutions are included, but first write the free-body diagram and predict the trend.

C1 · A support solution that cannot occur

Conceptual · Lectures 2 and 4 · Tests reaction admissibility

Fig. 1.8 — Computed reactions as the tip load P increases on the 4 m supported span with a 2 m overhang. A negative left reaction exposes the need for a hold-down.

A beam rests on two unanchored supports at x = 0 and x = 4 m and extends to x = 6 m. A downward load P acts at the overhanging tip. Explain why the equilibrium equations have a unique solution but the assumed resting configuration cannot persist for any positive P. What single modeling change could make the solution feasible?

Read the full solution

Moments about the left support give , hence . Vertical equilibrium then gives . An unanchored support can push up but cannot pull down, so that reaction is inadmissible. The rigid beam begins to lift from the left support under this idealization. A hold-down capable of exerting the required downward force would make the algebraic support state feasible. The force solution is determinate; contact feasibility is the missing condition.

D1 · Toggle force and motion are reciprocal

Derivational · Lecture 5 · Tests compatible virtual work

Fig. 1.9 — The toggle’s half-span a and centre height y form a right triangle of fixed hypotenuse ℓ. A downward centre displacement is compatible with two outward endpoint displacements.

Two equal links of fixed length ℓ join a centre joint at height y above two horizontally guided outer joints. Let a be each half-span, so . Derive the horizontal output force at each outer joint under a downward input P at the centre using both joint equilibrium and compatible small-displacement work.

Read the full solution

At the centre, each compressed link has upward component C sin θ. Thus C = P/(2 sin θ), and Q = C cos θ = P/(2 tan θ). For the work route, differentiate the length constraint: . A downward centre movement has dy < 0 and outward outputs have da > 0. Positive input work is −P dy; total work against two output loads is 2Q da. Therefore . Substitute and cancel the nonzero displacement to obtain Q = Pa/(2y). Since tan θ = y/a, this agrees with the force result. Both outer outputs must be counted.

K1 · Find the angle at which a toggle exceeds a link limit

Computational investigation · Lecture 5 · Tests an inverse threshold

Fig. 1.10 — Computed compression and outward force for P = 300 N. The 1500 N compression threshold occurs at 5.7392°, before the mathematical straight-link singularity.

For P = 300 N, each link must remain below 1500 N compression in this ideal force model. Sweep θ from 5° to 30° and find the minimum admissible angle. How much outward force does each side supply at that boundary? Explain which design checks are still missing.

Read the full solution

The compression condition is , giving sin θ ≥ 0.1 and . At that boundary Q = 1500 cos θ = 1492.48 N per side. At 5° the compression is 1721.06 N and violates the stated limit; at 30° it is 300 N. The plotted curve is computed directly from the geometry-based equation. Pin stress, elastic changes in angle, buckling, and friction remain separate questions.

Lecture 6

Introduction - Truss Structures

Setup and symbols.

We now apply the two-force-member result to every bar in a truss. The integers m, j, and r count members, joints, and unknown support-reaction components. The signed quantity denotes the axial force in bar AC: positive means tension, negative means compression. A stable geometry restrains the relevant small motions; a determinate force problem has enough independent equilibrium equations for a unique solution. Those are separate tests.

The ideal truss model

A truss carries loads through a network of bars. In the ideal model, each bar is straight, each connection is a frictionless pin, and external loads enter at the joints. Member weight is neglected or represented by suitable joint loads. Every bar is then a two-force member, so its internal force is axial. This is the reason joint equilibrium works: the direction of each unknown member force is already known from geometry.

Real connections have finite size and may transfer some moment. Real roof loads can act between joints. The truss model is most useful when these departures have a small effect on the axial load path. If a substantial transverse load acts midway along a bar, that bar must also resist bending. Simply moving the load to a joint changes the local problem and needs justification.

A triangular arrangement is geometrically rigid in its own plane when its three bar lengths are fixed. A four-sided pin-connected loop can change shape without changing side lengths. A diagonal usually removes that freedom. This geometric difference explains why triangulation is common, but it is not a substitute for checking the actual support arrangement and member geometry.

Counting unknowns and recognizing the limit of counting

Let m be the number of members, j the number of joints, and r the number of unknown reaction components in a planar truss. There are two force equations per joint. A necessary count for a statically determinate stable truss is

For common pin-and-roller support with r = 3, this becomes m = 2j minus 3. Equality does not prove stability. Some equations can be dependent because of member alignment, and a redundant region can coexist with a mechanism elsewhere. A geometric inspection or a rank check is needed when the arrangement is unusual. If a stable truss has more independent force unknowns than equations, deformation compatibility is required to determine the forces.

The sign convention that simplifies every joint

Assume an unknown member is in tension and draw its force away from the isolated joint along the member. Keep that assumption consistently at both ends. A positive solved value confirms tension. A negative value means compression and reverses the actual arrow. The signed unknown describes the same member force at either end; the direction vectors are opposite.

Our reference triangular truss

Let A = (0,0) m, B = (6,0) m, and C = (3,4) m. Members AB, AC, and BC form a triangle. A is pinned and B supplies a vertical roller reaction. A downward 10 kN load acts at C. Each inclined member is 5 m long, so its horizontal and vertical direction ratios are 3/5 and 4/5.

Fig. 2.1 — Geometry and external apex load. Ideal pin at A and vertical roller at B. Coordinates are in metres; the drawing is schematic.

For the complete truss, symmetry gives equal vertical reactions, but we should still be able to derive them. Moments about A give , hence . Vertical equilibrium gives the same value at A, and . The support system has three independent components and prevents rigid-body translation and rotation.

With three members, three reactions, and three joints, the count gives 3 + 3 = 2(3). This small triangle is stable and determinate. We will solve its members in the next lecture, then use its geometry to understand how height affects forces.

Loads and member sizes are different questions

Statics gives the axial force demanded by a load case. It does not give the permissible stress or the buckling load. A tensile bar can be checked against tensile strength and connection capacity. A compressive bar may buckle even when its average compressive stress is modest. Therefore, identifying compression is more than a sign-labeling exercise; it tells the later design analysis which failure mechanisms deserve attention.

If all external loads are scaled by the same factor while the geometry and active supports remain unchanged, the forces in a determinate linear equilibrium model scale by that factor. This proportionality is another useful check. It fails if a cable slackens, a contact opens, or a different structural configuration is activated.

What the member count actually counts

Proposition: the usual planar count is a necessary independence condition.

For j pin joints, m axial members, and r reaction components, a square joint-equilibrium system has . This statement does not by itself assert stability.

Fig. 2.2 — A pin-connected quadrilateral can change shape at fixed side lengths. The diagonal supplies a length constraint that the four boundary bars do not.

Each joint contributes two scalar force equations, giving 2j rows. Each bar needs one signed force unknown, and each independent support component needs one more, giving m + r columns. A unique solution to a square system requires its columns and rows to be independent. Geometry can make the matrix rank smaller than its row count, so merely equating the counts cannot establish uniqueness.

In an ordinary supported truss with three reaction components, the count reduces to m = 2j − 3. A four-bar quadrilateral with no diagonal can change shape at fixed side lengths; a diagonal generally removes that motion. The drawing makes the missing geometric restraint visible.

∎

Lecture 7

Truss Structures - Method of Joints

Setup and symbols.

Using the model established in Lecture 6, isolate one joint. A positive member force points away from that joint. P is the downward apex load, L the total horizontal span, h the apex height, and the sloping bar’s angle above horizontal. C is a positive compression magnitude; T is the bottom tie’s positive tension magnitude. C and T here are magnitudes, unlike the signed member variables and .

Solve the equilibrium of one joint at a time

An ideal joint is treated as a particle. All member forces pass through it, so a moment equation about the joint is automatically zero and supplies no new information. In a plane, each joint provides a horizontal and a vertical equation. A joint with no more than two unknown nonparallel member forces is a useful starting point.

Before solving members, find reactions from the complete truss whenever that is convenient. Then choose a joint with the fewest remaining unknowns. Transfer each solved signed member force to the next joint using the appropriate direction vector. Continue until the requested forces are known. A joint left until the end often provides a valuable independent check.

Worked example: the triangular truss

Use the truss introduced in Lecture 6. At joint A, the known upward reaction is 5 kN. Assume both AC and AB are tensile. AC therefore points right and up from A; AB points right. The equations are

AC is in compression and AB is in tension. At C, a tensile AC force would point down and left, but its negative value means the actual force points up and right. Applying the same signed-force convention to BC gives . The two compression forces supply vertical components of 5 kN each and cancel horizontally, balancing the 10 kN load.

At B, AB pulls left with 3.75 kN. Compressive BC pushes down its member direction toward B, which is right and down from C, but the force on joint B is away from C: right and down. Its downward component is 5 kN and its rightward component is 3.75 kN. Together with the upward support reaction, the joint balances. This verbal direction check is useful because the same compressed member points differently on the diagrams of its two end joints.

General derivation: how height changes member force

For a symmetric triangular truss of total span L, height h, and downward apex load P, each support carries P/2. Let the inclined member angle above the horizontal be theta. The inclined force magnitude C and bottom tie tension T follow from joint equilibrium:

The tie force grows inversely with height. A shallower truss does not make the load disappear; it produces larger opposing horizontal components to obtain the same vertical support. For the example, L = 6 m and h = 4 m give T = 3.75 kN. Reducing h to 2 m while holding L and P fixed doubles the tie force to 7.5 kN.

This relationship explains a recurring structural tradeoff. Greater depth often lowers chord forces, but uses more space and changes member lengths, weight, and stability. Statics exposes the force trend; it does not by itself choose an optimal structure.

When the usual progression gets stuck

Some determinate trusses have no convenient joint with only two unknowns at the stage you reach. That does not automatically make the structure indeterminate. You can solve several joint equations simultaneously or use the method of sections to obtain one strategic force. The decision should reduce algebra while preserving a clear free-body diagram.

Write direction cosines from coordinates rather than from a crowded drawing. If a bar goes from joint i to joint j, subtract coordinates, divide by the bar length, and multiply by its signed force. This method extends directly to space trusses and avoids repeatedly guessing angle quadrants.

Accuracy and residuals

Carry exact fractions or adequate digits during intermediate calculations. Rounding a direction ratio too early can leave a noticeable imbalance at a final joint. A residual is the vector sum of all forces after substituting the solution. It should be zero up to numerical precision. A small residual caused by rounding differs from a systematic error such as using the same arrow direction at both ends of a member.

Derive the complete height dependence

Proposition: a symmetric triangle’s tie force is inversely proportional to its height.

For a fixed span L, positive height h, and central downward load P, the tie tension is .

Fig. 2.3 — Computed tie and slope-member forces for an 8 m span carrying a 12 kN apex load. The inset defines the height and half-span; the plot shows the distinct force trends.

Each reaction is P/2 by whole-truss force and moment equilibrium. At a support joint, the compressed slope bar’s downward component is C sin θ; therefore C sin θ = P/2. Its horizontal component must be balanced by the tie, so T = C cos θ. Divide the two component equations to obtain T = (P/2) cot θ. Geometry gives tan θ = h/(L/2), hence cot θ = L/(2h), and substitution gives the stated result.

The first expression follows by using sin θ = h divided by the slope-bar length. As h increases without bound, C approaches P/2; it does not approach zero. As h approaches zero, both force magnitudes diverge, signaling the nearly unrestrained transverse direction.

Lecture 8

Truss Structures - Method of Sections

Setup and symbols.

Lecture 7 found forces joint by joint. A section instead isolates several joints and the connecting material as one body. Each cut member contributes one signed axial force, named by its endpoints, such as . A positive value pulls away from the retained portion. The reference point for moments need not lie inside that portion. The example uses metre coordinates and kilonewton forces.

A cut exposes only the member forces you need

The method of joints is efficient when many forces are required. If only one interior member is of interest, solving all preceding joints can be unnecessary. Instead, make an imaginary cut through members, retain one portion of the truss, and replace every cut bar by its axial force. The retained portion is a rigid-body free-body diagram, so it supplies two force equations and one moment equation in a plane.

Assume tensile forces pointing away from the retained portion. A negative result then means compression, just as in the joint method. The full truss reactions remain external loads on whichever retained portion includes their supports. Do not include forces at joints lying entirely within the retained portion: those are internal and cancel.

Why moment centres matter

If two of the cut-member lines meet at a point, taking moments about that point eliminates their unknowns. The third force can then be found directly if its line does not pass through the same point. The moment centre may lie outside the physical truss. It is a mathematical reference point, not a required support or material location.

The familiar advice to cut no more than three unknown members is a useful default, not an absolute rule. A cut through more members can still reveal one target force if all the other unknown lines pass through a common point. Conversely, three cut unknowns may not be individually solvable if their geometry makes the equilibrium equations dependent.

Worked example: a two-panel truss

Define bottom joints A = (0,0), B = (4,0), C = (8,0) m and top joints D = (2,3), E = (6,3) m. Members are AB, BC, AD, DB, BE, EC, and DE. A is pinned, C has a vertical roller, and downward 12 kN loads act at D and E. The complete truss is symmetric, so each vertical reaction is 12 kN and the horizontal reaction is zero.

Fig. 2.4 — The section crosses DE, DB, and AB. Retain the A–D portion and take moments about B to eliminate two cut forces.

Cut through AB, DB, and DE, retaining the portion containing A and D. To find DE, take moments about B. The AB and DB lines pass through B and disappear from the equation. The reaction at A creates a clockwise 48 kN m moment. The load at D creates a counterclockwise 24 kN m moment. A positive tensile DE force acts right at height 3 m and creates a clockwise moment:

Thus DE is compressed. Notice how choosing B avoided finding AD or any other internal member. AD lies entirely within the retained body and contributes no external force to its diagram.

Recovering the other cut forces

The direction from D to B is (2, minus 3), with length square root of 13 m. Vertical equilibrium of the retained body gives

Horizontal equilibrium then gives , so AB carries 8 kN in tension. The zero diagonal is a result for this particular load case, not a declaration that the member is useless or may be removed under all conditions.

How to choose the retained side

Both sides of a cut contain the same member-force information. Prefer the side with fewer applied loads, fewer unknown reactions, or simpler moment arms. If the smaller-looking side contains an unknown support reaction while the other side does not, the visually larger side may be easier. Efficiency follows the equations, not the amount of steel in the sketch.

After obtaining a section result, check one force through a joint if practical. Two methods agreeing on the same member provide stronger evidence than repeating the same algebra. The next lecture changes the load pattern on this same truss and shows how much of the solution can be reused without assuming symmetry that no longer exists.

Back to module start

Lecture 9

Truss Structures - Method of Sections (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

Retain the geometry and cut from Lecture 8, but let P and Q denote the downward loads at D and E respectively. are the upward support-reaction components. are signed axial forces, with tension positive. In the later beam comparison, M is an internal bending moment and h is the perpendicular separation between approximately opposite chord forces. This comparison is an estimate unless the force geometry justifies exact equality.

Editorial continuation: unsymmetrical loads and force formulas

The syllabus names a second section-method lecture without specifying its subdivision. Here it develops the previous truss under unequal loads and derives formulas that reveal how the load path changes. The geometry and member list remain exactly those in Lecture 8, but the downward loads at D and E are now P and Q.

Whole-truss equilibrium gives

These expressions follow from the load coordinates 2 m and 6 m on an 8 m span. They are force formulas, so P and Q must use the same force unit. Setting P = Q immediately recovers equal reactions. Setting Q = 0 produces the larger reaction on the left, nearer P.

Derive the cut forces without solving every joint

Use the same left portion and the same moment centre B as before. Its moment equation becomes

The denominator 3 comes from the 3 m truss height after cancellation of consistent length units. Vertical equilibrium gives

Horizontal equilibrium then gives

The top chord DE depends on the sum of the loads. The diagonal DB depends on their difference. This is a useful physical distinction: one member carries a global bending-related action, while the diagonal responds to the unbalanced panel loading. Such interpretations emerge naturally after a symbolic solution.

Worked example: one load doubles

Let P = 18 kN and Q = 6 kN. The reactions are 15 kN at A and 9 kN at C. The formulas give DE = minus 8 kN, DB = minus square root of 13 kN, approximately minus 3.606 kN, and AB = 10 kN. The diagonal is now compressed rather than unloaded.

Substitute the values into the retained-body equations. Vertically, the reaction minus the applied load is minus 3 kN, while the compressed DB member supplies plus 3 kN. Horizontally, AB contributes plus 10 kN, DB contributes minus 2 kN, and DE contributes minus 8 kN. Both residuals vanish. The moment check about B gives minus 60 plus 36 plus 24 kN m, also zero.

If P and Q are interchanged, the top chord remains at minus 8 kN but DB becomes tensile. A member can reverse between tension and compression under different loading. That fact matters when choosing slender members, connections, or tension-only bracing.

Connection to beam behavior

In a deeper truss, a smaller chord force can produce the same moment because the separation between top and bottom chord forces is larger. In the simple idealization of two opposite chord forces separated by depth h, their couple magnitude is approximately Fh. Thus an internal bending moment M is associated with a chord force scale M/h. This is a useful estimate, not a universal exact formula for every chord at every joint. Inclination, panel geometry, and shear-carrying members affect the detailed result.

This connection prepares the transition to beams. A truss resolves internal action into forces in distinct bars. A beam distributes internal action continuously through a cross section. Both can transmit a net internal force and moment across an imagined cut.

Sections that fail and how to repair them

Suppose a cut passes through three member lines that all meet at one point. Taking moments there eliminates all three, so it cannot distinguish their magnitudes. The remaining two force equations are insufficient for three unknowns unless some additional information is known. Choose another cut, solve a nearby joint first, or assemble a larger simultaneous system.

A cut is a tool for obtaining independent equations. It has no special power merely because it crosses three bars. Always inspect the geometry of the force lines and ask which unknown each proposed equation will actually constrain.

Lecture 10

Truss Structures - Zero Force Members

Setup and symbols.

The section equations showed one way a force can vanish. We now derive local zero-force rules from joint equilibrium. A joint is “unloaded” only if no applied force or support reaction acts there. Collinear means lying on exactly the same straight line. P denotes the specified downward joint load; is the signed axial force in member CD. “Zero” always refers to the stated load case and idealization.

Zero is a precise result for a stated load case

A zero-force member has zero axial force under the particular idealized loading being considered. It may still stabilize the geometry, brace a compressed member, carry another load case, or carry self-weight omitted from the model. Therefore, finding zero force is an analytical simplification, not an automatic instruction to remove the bar.

Two common rules follow directly from joint equilibrium. At an unloaded joint with exactly two noncollinear members and no support reaction, both member forces are zero. At an unloaded joint with exactly three members, if two are collinear and the third is not, the noncollinear member has zero force. The qualifications about load and reaction are essential.

Derivation of the two-member rule

Choose one coordinate axis along the first member. The other noncollinear member has a nonzero perpendicular component. With no external force, perpendicular equilibrium forces its axial force to zero. Equilibrium along the first member then forces that member's force to zero as well. If the members are collinear, this argument fails: equal and opposite axial forces can pass through the joint.

Derivation of the three-member rule

Choose an axis along the two collinear members. Only the third member contributes perpendicular force. Its perpendicular component must vanish, so its axial force is zero. The two collinear forces need not be zero; they transmit equal axial action through the joint. This derivation also shows a useful generalization: an external load parallel to the collinear pair does not alter the conclusion about the third member, provided no other perpendicular force acts.

Worked example: a split triangle

Fig. 2.5 — Geometry and external apex load. Ideal pin at A and vertical roller at B. Coordinates are in metres; the drawing is schematic.

Let A = (0,0), D = (3,0), B = (6,0), and C = (3,4) m. Members AD and DB form the bottom chord, AC and BC form the sides, and CD is vertical. A is pinned and B has a vertical roller. A downward load P acts at C; no load acts at D.

At D, AD and DB are collinear and CD is not. Therefore CD has zero force. The remaining truss force solution is the same as for the unsplit triangle: each side is compressed by 5P/8 and each bottom segment is tensile by 3P/8. For P = 10 kN, those values are 6.25 kN compression and 3.75 kN tension.

Now move the same load from C to D. At D, the downward load must be balanced by the upward tensile force in CD, so . At C, CD pulls downward, and the side bars support it. The side and bottom forces happen to retain the same magnitudes in this particular geometry, but CD has changed from zero to P. A visual zero-force rule applied without checking the changed load would miss the entire load path into the truss.

Apply rules iteratively, but preserve the model

After identifying a zero-force member, it may be omitted from the force-balance sketch of a neighboring joint for that load case. This can expose a second zero-force pattern. Continue until no further deduction follows. Keep the physical member in the structural model when discussing stability or another load case.

Do not apply the unloaded-joint rule at a support unless the reaction is known to vanish or is included explicitly. Likewise, two members that look nearly collinear in a drawing are not exactly collinear unless the geometry says so. A very small angle can require a large force to supply a finite transverse component; replacing “small” by “zero” can fundamentally change the equations.

A zero force can be discovered without a visual rule

In Lecture 8, DB vanished under equal top loads even though its zero-force status was most directly obtained from a section equation. The local rules are sufficient conditions, not a complete classification. Symmetry or global load balance can produce zero member force in cases where no familiar joint pattern appears immediately.

Finish a truss analysis by stating the load case alongside the force table. Report tension, compression, and zero explicitly. A list of signed numbers without the declared sign convention is less useful to the next person who must interpret the structural behavior.

Truss Structures - Method of Sections

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

Use the two-panel truss of Lecture 9 with P = 6 kN and Q = 18 kN. Find DE, DB, and AB.

Open a hint

Retain the A–D side and take moments about B.

Read the full solution

The reactions are 9 kN at A and 15 kN at C. The moment equation gives DE = −8 kN. Vertical balance gives kN in tension, approximately 3.606 kN. Horizontal balance gives AB = 6 kN in tension. The retained-side horizontal sum is 6 + 2 − 8 = 0.

Problem 2

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A planar section crosses three unknown bars whose lines all pass through one point. Why might three equilibrium equations fail to determine all three?

Open a hint

Consider moments about their common intersection.

Read the full solution

All three unknowns have zero moment about that point. The moment equation supplies no coefficient for any of them. Only two independent force equations remain for three magnitudes. Solve another joint, choose another cut, or add genuinely independent information. Merely recounting three written equations does not restore independence.

Truss Structures - Zero Force Members

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

At an unloaded joint, two bars are horizontal and collinear, and a third is at 45 degrees. Find the third force. Then add a downward 4 kN joint load and find it again.

Open a hint

Use vertical equilibrium in both cases.

Read the full solution

Without load, the inclined force is zero. With the load and the inclined bar pointing upward from the joint under a tensile assumption, , so in tension. The horizontal bars must together balance its 4 kN horizontal component; their individual forces need further information.

Problem 2

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A bar is zero-force under one symmetric gravity load case. Give two reasons it might still be retained.

Open a hint

Separate load-case force from stability and other demands.

Read the full solution

It may carry an unsymmetrical, wind, or construction load case. It may also restrain a joint motion or brace a compressed member against buckling. Zero axial force in one ideal load case does not imply no structural function.

Practice problems

Use these as an untimed problem set. A complete answer includes the isolated body, force directions, equations, units, and a physical check.

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A planar truss has 6 joints, 9 bars, and 3 independent reaction components. What does the count establish?

Open a hint

Distinguish a necessary count from a proof of rigidity.

Read the full solution

The equality 9 + 3 = 2(6) is satisfied. The truss could be statically determinate if the geometry is stable and the equations independent. The count alone cannot exclude a mechanism or a locally redundant arrangement.

Problem 2

Open a hint

Read the full solution

The reactions are 9 and 3 kN. , , and . At the left retained body, vertical forces are 9 − 12 + 3 = 0 and horizontal forces are 6 − 2 − 4 = 0.

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

The triangular truss has span 10 m, height 2 m, and apex load 8 kN. Find tie tension and slope compression.

Open a hint

The half-span is 5 m.

Read the full solution

Tie tension is . Each slope carries compression. Its vertical component is 4 kN and horizontal component 10 kN.

An unloaded two-member joint has two bars exactly collinear. Must both forces be zero?

Module 2 assessment and solutions

Original counterpart of the syllabus’s graded assessment: Plane Trusses . Work without viewing solutions, then review. Suggested self-assessment: 4 points for modeling and equations, 4 for results and units, and 2 for checks per question; 30 points total. No institutional grade or credential is issued.

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A symmetric triangular truss has span 6 m, height 3 m, and apex load 18 kN downward. Find all member forces.

Read the full solution

Each reaction is 9 kN. Each inclined bar has 45-degree inclination and carries compression. The bottom tie carries 9 kN tension. The apex vertical components add to 18 kN.

Problem 2

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

Use Lecture 9 geometry with P = Q = 9 kN. Find DE, DB, and AB.

Read the full solution

DE = −6 kN, DB = 0, and AB = 6 kN. Each support reaction is 9 kN. Moments about B on the retained left side give −36 + 18 − 3DE = 0.

Problem 3

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

Why are three force equations unavailable at a planar truss joint?

Read the full solution

A planar joint has two independent force components. All member and applied joint forces pass through it, so its moment equation about the joint is identically zero. Moment equations become useful for an extended section containing separated joints.

Extension problems: stability and force reversal

C2 · Equal counts, different restraint

Conceptual · Lectures 6 and 10 · Tests geometry versus counting

Fig. 2.6 — A pin-connected quadrilateral can change shape at fixed side lengths. The diagonal supplies a length constraint that the four boundary bars do not.

Explain why “m + r = 2j, therefore stable” is invalid. Give the mechanical interpretation of a direction of motion that does not change bar lengths to first order.

Read the full solution

The count only compares equation and unknown numbers. Independence depends on the geometry. If a small joint displacement is perpendicular to each connected bar in the first-order length-change equations, the bars do not stretch to first order along that motion. Such an infinitesimal mechanism can coexist with an apparently correct global count. A rank check of the compatibility or equilibrium system, together with attention to support restraint and possible higher-order effects, is stronger than counting alone.

D2 · Prove the diagonal’s force-reversal rule

Derivational · Lectures 8–9 · Tests section equilibrium

Fig. 2.7 — For fixed total load P + Q = 24 kN in the Lecture 9 truss, the diagonal DB reverses sign at P = 12 kN while top chord DE remains compressed at 8 kN.

For the two-panel truss of Lecture 9, derive DB’s force directly from the left retained body. Then hold P + Q fixed and show exactly where DB changes from compression to tension.

Read the full solution

Whole-truss moments and forces give . On the A–D side, downward P and the assumed tensile DB component oppose Ay, so . Therefore . Under fixed total S = P + Q, replace Q by S − P: . The force vanishes at P = S/2, is tensile below that value, and compressive above it. This reasoning uses a bar that can carry both signs. A tension-only replacement may deactivate when the sign becomes negative.

K2 · Choose truss height under a tie-force limit

Computational investigation · Lecture 7 · Tests inverse design and competing force trends

Fig. 2.8 — Computed tie and slope-member forces for an 8 m span carrying a 12 kN apex load. The inset defines the height and half-span; the plot shows the distinct force trends.

A symmetric triangular truss has span 8 m and apex load 12 kN. Its tie-force limit is 6 kN. Sweep height h from 1 m to 6 m. Find the minimum height allowed by that limit and the slope-bar compression there. Does raising the height indefinitely make every member force vanish?

Read the full solution

The tie force is T = 24/h kN when h is entered in metres. Thus h ≥ 4 m. At h = 4 m, the slope-bar compression is kN. As height increases, T tends to zero but the compression tends to 6 kN, the required upward component at each support. The problem establishes only a tie-force condition. Increasing height also changes bar length, weight, clearance, and buckling behavior.
