Space trusses and beams

Space Trusses; Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams

Lectures 11–17 · Original textbook course · Offline edition · 9 September 2026

Read the chapters in order. Work each example independently, then use the worksheets and practice set. Solutions open on demand. Repeated “continued” lecture subdivisions are editorial choices, explicitly labeled in the text.
Lecture 11

Space Trusses

Setup and symbols.

The joint method now extends from two coordinates to three. are position vectors; means the Euclidean length of vector . The unit vector points from A toward B and has length one. The scalar is a signed member force. Multiplying that scalar by gives its vector on joint A. The letters x, y, z label mutually perpendicular coordinate axes.

What changes when the structure leaves the plane

A space truss is an assembly of ideal two-force bars whose joints do not all lie in one plane. The member force still acts along the member, and tension remains positive. The change is that each joint now supplies three force equations. A sketch projected onto a page can conceal the true geometry, so coordinates are usually more reliable than apparent angles.

For a member from A to B, form the displacement vector and divide by its length:

The three components of the unit vector are direction cosines. Their squares sum to one. This provides a quick check on a transcription error. The member's signed scalar force multiplies the unit vector pointing away from the joint under analysis.

Particle equations and whole-structure equations

At a joint,

A moment equation about the joint again adds no information because all forces are concurrent. For the complete spatial assembly, however, three force and three moment equations are generally available. A support system must restrain all relevant rigid-body motions. A collection of bars may be internally rigid yet inadequately supported as a whole.

For a spatial pin-jointed truss, the corresponding necessary count is m + r = 3j for a statically determinate arrangement, with support reactions included. As in the plane, equality alone proves neither rigidity nor independence. Coplanar or specially aligned bars can leave a joint unable to resist a force in some direction.

Worked example: a symmetric three-bar support

Let an upper joint O lie at (0,0,3) m. It connects to ground joints A = (2,0,0), B = (minus 1, square root of 3,0), and C = (minus 1, minus square root of 3,0) m. Each bar has length square root of 13 m. A downward 9 kN load acts at O. The ground joints are fixed in position by supports outside the isolated joint model.

Fig. 3.1 — Computed orthographic projection of the actual symmetric three-bar coordinates in Lecture 11. The dashed triangle marks the anchor plane; it is not three additional truss members.

By rotational symmetry, all three member forces have the same signed value F. Their horizontal components cancel. Their upward support must come from compression, since tensile forces at O would point down toward the anchors. The vertical equation is

Each bar carries approximately 3.606 kN compression. Its vertical component on O is 3 kN upward. The horizontal magnitude of each force is 2 kN, and the three horizontal vectors sum to zero because they are 120 degrees apart.

Why this example is more than a symmetry trick

The force directions were known before any force magnitude was calculated. That is the defining advantage of the truss idealization. If the same three elements were cables leading down to ground anchors, they could not support a downward load at O without another supporting action. The algebra would demand negative cable tensions. With bars, compression is permitted; with cables, that result invalidates the assumed system.

The example analyzes equilibrium of the upper joint with fixed lower endpoints. A full design would also determine forces on the ground supports and check each bar for buckling. The negative sign alone says nothing about the compression capacity.

How to organize a larger space truss

Create a coordinate table, a member-connectivity list, and a support list. For each joint, assemble its connected member unit vectors. Use one signed unknown per member throughout the structure. If all member forces are needed, a matrix solution is often less error-prone than a long hand sequence, but a few joints should still be checked independently. Computation removes arithmetic labor; it does not decide whether a support reaction or missing member was modeled correctly.

Back to module start

Lecture 12

Space Trusses (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

Lecture 11 used symmetry; this lecture solves unequal spatial forces. denote the axial forces in the bars from O toward A, B, C. The auxiliary quantities are force divided by member length, with units of kN/m. In , U is the matrix whose columns are member unit vectors, is the column of member-force magnitudes, and is the applied-force column.

Editorial continuation: an unsymmetrical spatial joint

We now solve a spatial joint without relying on equal member forces. Put O at the origin. Its three bars point toward A = (2,0,3), B = (0,2,3), and C = (minus 2,minus 2,3) m. Their lengths are square root of 13, square root of 13, and square root of 17 m. An external force of (2, minus 1, minus 12) kN acts at O. The remote endpoints are held fixed.

Instead of carrying the square roots through every equation, define qA = FA divided by square root of 13, qB = FB divided by square root of 13, and qC = FC divided by square root of 17. These scaled quantities are bookkeeping variables, not new physical forces. The three equilibrium equations become

The first two give qA = qC minus 1 and qB = qC plus 0.5. Substitute into the third: 9qC minus 1.5 equals 12, so qC = 1.5, qA = 0.5, and qB = 2. In the numerical coordinate convention used here, the recovered axial forces are

All are positive, hence tensile. The force vectors contributed by the bars are (1,0,1.5), (0,4,6), and (minus 3,minus 3,4.5) kN. Their sum is (minus 2,1,12) kN, exactly opposite the applied force. Checking the component vectors is clearer than checking rounded magnitudes alone.

Matrix form makes the geometry visible

Place the three member unit vectors in the columns of a matrix U. The equilibrium problem is

Here f contains the three member magnitudes and p is the applied force vector. A unique solution exists if the columns are linearly independent. Three nonparallel bars can still fail this test if all three lie in a common plane through the joint. They then cannot supply a resultant normal to that plane.

For a small hand calculation, elimination is enough. For a numerical calculation, solving the linear system directly is preferable to explicitly calculating a matrix inverse. The important mechanical fact is not the computational method but whether the force directions span three-dimensional space.

A geometrically weak direction

Suppose all three bars become nearly horizontal while a fixed vertical load remains. Their vertical direction cosines become small. Large axial forces may then be required to create modest vertical components. The equilibrium matrix becomes poorly conditioned: small changes in geometry or load can cause large changes in the solution.

This is the spatial version of the shallow truss and near-straight toggle. Different-looking structures share the same underlying limitation: the available force directions have little component in the direction that needs support. Recognizing this pattern helps predict large forces before calculation.

Tension-only interpretation

If the elements in this example are cables rather than bars, the positive solution is admissible for the idealized joint. However, arbitrary changes in the applied load may make one solved force negative. In that event, remove the assumption that all three cables remain taut and analyze the appropriate active set, if any. A negative cable value cannot simply be relabeled compression.

The set of loads supportable by positive cable tensions forms a cone generated by the cable direction vectors, with the applied load opposite that cone. This is an optional geometric viewpoint, but it explains why cable-supported joints can resist some load directions and not others even when the linear equation matrix is invertible.

Restore units to the scaled unknowns

Dividing force by member length is useful, but it changes units. In the earlier equations the coordinate numbers were entered in metres. Written dimensionally, the x equation is . Thus qA = 0.5 kN/m, qB = 2 kN/m, and qC = 1.5 kN/m. Multiplying by the actual lengths in metres recovers the stated forces in kilonewtons. A unit vector is dimensionless; an unnormalized displacement vector is not.

Fig. 3.2 — Computed orthographic projection of the actual coordinates in Lecture 12. The three column directions in the equilibrium matrix correspond to the three labeled bars.

What a small residual cannot establish

The residual measures how closely the computed forces satisfy the entered equations. It does not measure how accurately the entered geometry represents the real structure. For example, if all three bars have small vertical direction cosines, the solver can balance a downward load very accurately while requiring enormous axial forces. Check the direction span and force sensitivity as well as the residual.

Back to module start

Lecture 13

Space Trusses (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

Having solved a spatial joint, we now ask whether its solution is well constrained. The vectors are unit vectors along x, y, z. The cross product is the moment vector. A dot product with an axis unit vector selects moment about that axis. In the bar-extension relation, is extension, F axial force, L original length, E Young’s modulus, and A cross-sectional area; that A is not a joint label.

Editorial continuation: stability, checking, and whole-structure moments

A force solution is not the same as proof that a structure is stable. Equilibrium asks whether forces can balance in the stated geometry. Stability asks whether a small permitted motion or disturbance can occur and whether the system resists it. A structure can balance one special load while still being a mechanism under another disturbance.

Consider a joint connected to three bars all lying in the horizontal plane. Horizontal loads might be balanced. A vertical load cannot be balanced because all available member-force vertical components are zero. The joint also has an out-of-plane infinitesimal motion at that configuration. This simple example shows why a satisfied unknown count does not settle the question.

Worked example: compute a spatial moment explicitly

A force of (3, minus 2,5) kN acts at position (2,1,0) m relative to O. Its moment is the cross product

The x component is 1 times 5 minus 0 times minus 2. The y component is 0 times 3 minus 2 times 5. The z component is 2 times minus 2 minus 1 times 3. Writing these components separately prevents a sign error in the middle term of the determinant.

For the moment about a particular axis with unit vector e, take the scalar projection , choosing O on that axis. A moment vector may be nonzero while its moment about one chosen axis is zero. This distinction matters when a support restrains some rotations but not others.

A systematic verification procedure

After solving a space truss, reconstruct the vector sum at every free joint. Also reconstruct the total external force and moment of the complete structure, including reactions. Joint checks catch local sign and connectivity errors. Whole-structure checks catch missing external loads or incorrect reactions. Neither replaces the other.

Use a force scale such as the largest applied load to interpret numerical residuals. A residual of one millionth of a newton is negligible for a kilonewton problem; a residual of one kilonewton is not. For an ill-conditioned geometry, a tiny algebraic residual can coexist with highly sensitive force magnitudes. Therefore, residual and sensitivity checks answer different questions.

Geometry changes the force solution

For the symmetric support in Lecture 11, let each ground anchor be at radius r from the vertical axis and let the upper joint height be h. Each compressed bar has length square root of r squared plus h squared. Under downward load P,

At fixed r and P, reducing h increases C without bound as h approaches zero. If r approaches zero while h remains positive, the formula tends to P/3, but the three bars become coincident in direction and no longer restrain lateral motion. A reasonable axial force under one vertical load therefore does not prove a good three-dimensional support arrangement.

What comes after equilibrium

If the truss is statically indeterminate, member deformation and joint compatibility supply missing relationships. For a prismatic elastic bar, the axial extension is related to force through , where E is Young's modulus and A is cross-sectional area. We mention this relation to identify the missing information; a full stiffness-method course lies beyond this syllabus.

Likewise, a compressive-force table needs a later buckling and strength assessment. Statics determines the demand. It does not certify capacity. Knowing precisely what has and has not been solved is part of a rigorous engineering result.

The next four lectures retain the free-body method but change the object being cut. Instead of cutting slender axial bars, we cut beams and ask what total force and moment the material transmits across each section.

Back to module start

Lecture 14

Introduction – Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams

Setup and symbols.

We keep the cut-body method but now cut a beam. At section coordinate x, N is the axial-force resultant, V the transverse shear-force resultant, and M the bending-moment resultant. The function w is downward load per unit length. In the point-load example, L is span, a is load distance from the left support, b = L − a, P is the downward load, and are upward reactions. Superscripts + and − on a location mean values approached from its right and left, not positive and negative force.

What an internal cut means

Imagine separating a loaded beam at a location x. The material on one side previously exerted a distributed traction on the other. For planar equilibrium, that distributed interaction can be replaced at the cut by an axial force N, a transverse shear force V, and a bending moment M. These are resultants of internal stress, not three additional external loads applied to the intact beam.

A diagram plots how one of these resultants varies with x. It lets us find the largest internal demands and see where their signs change. The shear and moment diagrams depend on the external loading and supports. The conversion from these resultants to stress and deflection requires cross-sectional and material information studied in mechanics of materials.

Fix the sign convention before doing algebra

Take x positive to the right and distributed load w positive downward. On the right-hand cut face of a retained left beam segment, draw positive axial force to the right, positive shear downward, and positive bending moment counterclockwise. On the left-hand face of the retained right segment, all these actions reverse. Positive M is sagging: in the ordinary beam interpretation, the bottom fibres are stretched and the top fibres compressed.

Fig. 3.3 — Positive cut actions on the retained left beam segment: axial force right, shear down, bending moment counterclockwise. The opposite segment receives opposite actions.

The words “left face” and “left segment” are easily confused. Our positive shear is downward on the right face of the left segment. An infinitesimal element therefore has positive shear upward at its left end and downward at its right end. With this convention, the standard relationships derived in the next lectures are dV/dx = minus w and dM/dx = V.

Worked example: one point load

A simply supported beam has span L and a downward point load P at x = a. Let b = L minus a. Whole-beam equilibrium gives reactions RA = Pb/L and RB = Pa/L. For a cut to the left of the load, the retained left segment contains only RA and the cut actions. Its equilibrium gives

For a cut to the right of the load, include P at its actual position:

The moment is continuous at the point force because the load has zero lever arm as the cut approaches its application point. The shear drops by P. At x = L, moment becomes zero, consistent with the ideal end support. The peak moment occurs under the load and equals Pab/L.

Numerical interpretation

Take L = 6 m, P = 12 kN, and a = 2 m. Then RA = 8 kN and RB = 4 kN. The shear is plus 8 kN before the load and minus 4 kN after it. The moment rises linearly from zero to 16 kN m at x = 2 m and then falls linearly to zero at B. A maximum need not occur where a smooth shear curve crosses zero; here the shear jumps from positive to negative at the point load.

End supports and internal locations

An ideal pin at the physical end of a beam has zero end moment if no couple is applied there. A support located inside a continuous beam is different: the beam can transmit an internal moment across that location even if the support itself exerts no couple. Do not set M to zero at every roller symbol without checking whether the beam actually ends or has an internal hinge there.

When making a cut inside a distributed load, replace only the load on the retained segment by its resultant. Using the resultant of the full span would place some discarded loading back onto the isolated body and produce the wrong internal-force function.

Back to module start

Lecture 15

Shear Force Diagrams

Setup and symbols.

Use precisely the cut signs from Lecture 14. The short positive length dx separates two nearby sections; dV is the corresponding change in shear. The derivative dV/dx is the local rate of change of shear, and an integral of w is a load resultant. The coordinates a and b in an integral are its interval endpoints; c denotes the location of a concentrated load P. The notation distinguishes the value immediately right of that load from immediately left.

Derive the load–shear relationship

Isolate a short beam element from x to x + dx. On its left face the positive shear acts upward with magnitude V(x). On its right face it acts downward with magnitude V(x) + dV. The downward distributed force is approximately w(x) dx. Vertical equilibrium gives

The differential equation holds on intervals without concentrated forces. Integrating gives

Thus the signed area under a downward-load diagram is the decrease in shear. A region with no distributed load has constant shear. A uniform load gives a straight sloping shear line. A linearly varying load gives a quadratic shear curve.

Concentrated forces create jumps

A downward point force P at x = c creates . An upward reaction creates an upward jump of its magnitude. The left and right values are distinct at the idealized force location. Drawing a vertical connecting line indicates the jump; it does not represent a range of physically different shears at one ordinary cross section.

A pure applied couple does not create a shear jump because it adds no net vertical force. It will instead create a moment jump. Keeping these two effects separate is one of the simplest ways to avoid diagram errors.

Worked example: a uniform load over the whole span

A simply supported 8 m beam carries 3 kN/m downward. The total load is 24 kN and the reactions are 12 kN each. Beginning just to the right of A,

The shear starts at plus 12 kN, reaches zero at x = 4 m, and reaches minus 12 kN just before B. The 12 kN upward reaction then returns the exterior shear to zero. The slope is minus 3 kN/m, exactly the negative load intensity.

Worked example: a partial distributed load

A 6 m simply supported beam carries 2 kN/m only from x = 1 m to x = 4 m. The total is 6 kN at x = 2.5 m. Hence RB = 2.5 kN and RA = 3.5 kN. The shear is

At x = 1 and x = 4, the load intensity changes but there is no point force. The shear is continuous at those locations; only its slope changes. It crosses zero at x = 2.75 m. That position will be a candidate for a bending-moment maximum.

An efficient drawing sequence

First compute reactions. Mark every support, point force, couple, and change in distributed load on the x axis. Starting from a known shear value, use jumps at concentrated forces and signed areas between them. Annotate exact values at each breakpoint and each zero crossing. Finally, check that the net load over the entire beam is consistent with the final shear value.

If your shear does not return to the required end value, investigate before integrating it into a moment diagram. A moment diagram built from an incorrect shear curve can look smooth and plausible while inheriting the original mistake.

Shear is a resultant, not a stress

The unit of V is force. Dividing by area gives an average stress scale, but actual shear stress is generally not uniform across the section. Its distribution depends on geometry. In this course, the purpose of the shear diagram is to establish the internal resultant accurately; detailed stress formulas should not be silently substituted for this equilibrium step.

Separate a smooth load from a concentrated force

Proposition: load controls shear slope on smooth intervals and shear jumps at point loads.

With downward w positive, . A downward point force P causes .

Fig. 3.4 — Positive cut actions on a short beam element: shear is up on the left and down on the right, while moment is clockwise on the left and counterclockwise on the right. The applied intensity w acts downward.

For a finite interval from x to x + Δx containing no point force, vertical equilibrium of its isolated element reads . Here ξ is a dummy integration coordinate: it runs through the element while x labels its left end. Divide by Δx and take the limit as Δx tends to zero to obtain the derivative relation.

Now enclose a downward point force P in a shrinking interval. Its force does not shrink with the interval, while the distributed-load resultant does. The limiting equation is . Rearranging gives the jump. A change in w without a point force changes the slope but leaves V continuous.

∎

Back to module start

Lecture 16

Bending Moment Diagrams

Setup and symbols.

Lecture 15 related load to shear; we now relate shear to bending moment. M is positive sagging moment under the declared cut convention; dM is its change over dx. C is an externally applied couple, positive counterclockwise, at coordinate c. Here C is a couple magnitude, not the compression magnitude used in the truss chapter. A local extremum is a maximum or minimum relative to nearby sections; the largest absolute moment must be compared across the whole beam.

Derive the shear–moment relationship

Use the same short element and take moments about its left end. Positive moment is clockwise on the element's left face and counterclockwise on its right face. The right-end shear produces a clockwise moment. To first order,

The terms involving products of differentials vanish after division by dx in the limit. Therefore,

Combining this with the previous lecture gives . A downward positive load makes the moment curve concave downward. Where shear is positive, moment increases. Where shear is negative, moment decreases. At a smooth interior extremum, shear is zero.

Worked example: complete the uniformly loaded beam

For the 8 m beam under 3 kN/m, V = 12 minus 3x kN. Integrate and use M(0) = 0:

The maximum occurs at x = 4 m, where shear is zero. Substitution gives 24 kN m. The right-end value is 96 minus 96 = 0, as required. For a general simply supported span under uniform downward load w, this calculation gives

Doubling span at fixed load intensity multiplies the maximum moment by four. This is a central reason span length has such a strong effect on beam demand. The statement assumes the same simple support arrangement and the same load model.

Applied couples produce moment jumps

Let a positive counterclockwise external couple C act at x = c. Moment equilibrium of a shrinking element around it gives

This sign follows our declared internal-moment convention. A clockwise couple causes an upward jump. The shear remains continuous unless a point force also acts there. Some textbooks draw opposite moment conventions; a memorized jump direction without a convention is unsafe.

Worked example: a beam loaded only by a couple

A 4 m beam is pinned at A and supported by a vertical roller at B. A counterclockwise 6 kN m couple acts at x = 2 m. Whole-beam moments give , so B acts downward with 1.5 kN and A acts upward with 1.5 kN. This ideal reaction at B requires a support that can hold the beam down; an ordinary unanchored contact roller would lift off, invalidating the assumed support state.

The shear between supports is constant at plus 1.5 kN. The moment rises from zero to plus 3 kN m just before the couple, jumps down by 6 kN m to minus 3 kN m, then rises to zero at B. The area under shear over the span is 6 kN m, but the applied moment jump cancels it. Integrating shear alone across a concentrated couple without inserting the jump would give the wrong endpoint.

Boundary conditions are physical statements

At a free end without force or couple, both shear and moment vanish. At a free end carrying a point force, the adjacent internal shear is generally nonzero. At a fixed support, an unknown reaction couple usually produces a nonzero end moment. At an internal frictionless hinge, the transmitted bending moment is zero, although shear and axial force may be nonzero.

To locate the largest absolute moment, check smooth points where V = 0, points where shear changes sign by a jump, both sides of applied couples, and relevant endpoints. Checking only the zero-shear points can miss a governing support moment or moment discontinuity.

Moment jumps require their own balance

Proposition: a concentrated couple changes moment, not shear.

A positive counterclockwise couple C produces with the cut signs used here.

Fig. 3.5 — Computed moment on a 4 m simple beam carrying a counterclockwise 6 kN m couple at x = 2 m. The moment drops by 6 kN m while the shear remains 1.5 kN.

Enclose the couple in an element of length Δx. The positive internal moment on its left face acts clockwise, contributing −M⁻; on its right face it acts counterclockwise, contributing +M⁺. Include the external couple +C. Moments due to finite shear forces are proportional to Δx and vanish as the element shrinks. Therefore −M⁻ + M⁺ + C = 0, which gives the jump. Vertical equilibrium contains no force contribution from C, so V has no corresponding jump.

On an interval without such a couple, the finite shear moment survives at first order after dividing by Δx; this is the origin of dM/dx = V. Consequently, integrating V across a beam must be supplemented by all concentrated-couple jumps.

∎

Back to module start

Lecture 17

Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams – Examples

Setup and symbols.

We combine the jump and integration rules from Lectures 15–16. x measures distance from the left support or fixed end; L is total length. In the triangular-load example, , where k is a load gradient with units kN/m². It is not a force or a peak intensity. Positive V and M retain the earlier convention. A cantilever has one fixed end and one free end; an overhang extends beyond a support.

Example 1: combine a uniform load and an off-centre force

A simply supported 6 m beam carries 2 kN/m over its full span and a downward 6 kN force at x = 2 m. The distributed load totals 12 kN at x = 3 m. Moments about A give , hence RB = 8 kN and RA = 10 kN.

For 0 < x < 2 m, the left segment includes RA and the uniform load over length x. For 2 < x < 6 m, it also includes the point force. Therefore,

The shear is plus 6 kN just before the point load and zero just after it. For x greater than 2, it is negative. The moment therefore reaches its maximum at x = 2 m, with value 16 kN m. Both moment expressions give that value, proving continuity. At B, the moment is 60 minus 36 minus 24 = 0. The final shear is minus 8 kN, canceled by RB.

Fig. 3.6 — Lecture 17, Example 1: 2 kN/m over 6 m plus a 6 kN point load at x = 2 m. Positive moment is plotted upward; axes and key values are labeled.

This example shows why the phrase “set shear equal to zero” needs care. The governing point is a load discontinuity with a one-sided zero value, and it must be considered as a breakpoint even before solving a smooth derivative equation.

Example 2: a cantilever under a triangular load

A cantilever is fixed at x = 0 and free at x = L. A downward load varies as , where k has units of force per length squared. Apply the free-end conditions V(L) = 0 and M(L) = 0. Integrating the load–shear equation gives

Integrating again with the moment boundary condition gives

At the wall, V(0) = kL squared/2 and M(0) = minus kL cubed/3. The negative moment is hogging, consistent with a downward-loaded cantilever. Independently, the triangular load resultant is kL squared/2 and acts two-thirds of L from the wall. Its moment magnitude is kL cubed/3, confirming the support demand.

For L = 3 m and k = 2 kN/m squared, the load peaks at 6 kN/m, total load is 9 kN, and the wall moment is minus 18 kN m. The units matter: k is not itself the peak load intensity.

Example 3: an overhang creates a negative support-region moment

A beam is pinned at A, x = 0, and supported by a roller at B, x = 4 m. It continues to a free end C at x = 6 m, where a downward 8 kN force acts. Whole-beam equilibrium gives RB = 12 kN and RA = minus 4 kN. A must therefore be capable of exerting a downward reaction; an unanchored resting support would not sustain this load case.

Between A and B, shear is minus 4 kN and moment is minus 4x kN m. Thus M(B) = minus 16 kN m even though B is a roller. Between B and C, shear is plus 8 kN and moment is minus 16 + 8(x minus 4), returning to zero at C. The beam is continuous over B, so there is no internal hinge and no reason to set its section moment there to zero.

A disciplined final check

For every example, the reactions balance the complete load. Shear jumps match concentrated vertical forces. Moment jumps match applied couples with the declared sign. The moment slope equals shear on smooth intervals, and load intensity fixes shear slope. Boundary values agree with the physical supports and end loads. Finally, every required contact reaction has the permitted sign.

These checks are complementary. Satisfying the differential relations does not prove the support reactions were admissible. Satisfying global equilibrium does not prove the internal piecewise functions are correct. A textbook-quality solution closes both loops.

The unit-vector matrix is the identity.

Read the full solution

The first load requires tensile forces (2,3,4) kN. The second requires (−2,3,4) kN: the x bar is compressed. If these elements are cables, the second case has no equilibrium with all three taut. The invertible matrix does not override tension-only admissibility.

Module 3 assessment and solutions

Original counterpart of the syllabus’s graded assessment: Space Trusses; Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams . Work without viewing solutions, then review. Suggested self-assessment: 4 points for modeling and equations, 4 for results and units, and 2 for checks per question; 30 points total. No institutional grade or credential is issued.

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

For a 6 m simple beam under 4 kN/m, find V(x), M(x), and the maximum moment.

Read the full solution

Reactions are 12 kN each. kN and kN m. V vanishes at x = 3 m, where M = 18 kN m. Both end moments are zero.

Problem 2

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

At a spatial joint, three bar directions lie in one plane. Can they balance every possible 3D load?

Read the full solution

No. Their force vectors span at most that plane. A load component normal to it cannot be balanced. A special in-plane load may have equilibrium without proving full spatial restraint.

Problem 3

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A roller lies inside a continuous beam. Must the internal bending moment there be zero?

Read the full solution

No. The roller supplies no external couple, but the continuous beam can transfer internal moment across its cross section there. Zero transmitted moment follows from an actual internal hinge or an appropriate unloaded physical end, not from an interior roller alone.

Extension problems: sensitivity and discontinuities

C3 · A smooth-looking plot with the wrong physics

Conceptual · Lectures 15–16 · Tests concentrated actions

Fig. 3.7 — Computed moment on a 4 m simple beam carrying a counterclockwise 6 kN m couple at x = 2 m. The moment drops by 6 kN m while the shear remains 1.5 kN.

A computed moment curve is continuous through a nonzero concentrated couple. Its author reports a tiny residual for dM/dx = V everywhere else. Explain why that residual cannot validate the full solution.

Read the full solution

The derivative law applies on intervals without concentrated couples. A counterclockwise couple C imposes an independent jump . An implementation can integrate every smooth interval accurately yet omit the jump entirely. The local differential residual then misses the defect. Check both one-sided values and the global end conditions, not only derivatives away from singular loads.

D3 · Recover the point-load maximum without guessing its location

Derivational · Lecture 14 · Tests piecewise reasoning

Fig. 3.8 — A point load lies between two end supports. The distances a and L − a determine the reaction split and the peak moment directly under the load.

A simple span L has a downward load P at 0 < a < L. Derive the reactions and both moment intervals, then prove where the maximum occurs.

Read the full solution

Moments give , while vertical balance gives . Before the load, , with positive slope RA. After it, , with negative slope RA − P = −Pa/L. Therefore M increases before a and decreases after a, so its maximum is at a, even though shear does not pass smoothly through zero. Substitution gives . Both expressions agree at a, and M(L) = 0.

K3 · Sweep a moving point load

Computational investigation · Lecture 14 · Tests an influence trend and optimization

Fig. 3.9 — Computed peak bending moment for each separate position of a 12 kN load on a 6 m span. The most demanding position is midspan; the dashed level is 90% of that peak.

Move a 12 kN load across a 6 m simple span. Compute the peak moment for each load position a, identify the most demanding location, and find all positions giving at least 90% of that greatest peak.

Read the full solution

The peak for a fixed position is kN m. Its derivative is 12 − 4a, so the greatest value occurs at a = 3 m and equals 18 kN m. Requiring at least 16.2 kN m gives . The roots are , so the interval is 2.0513 to 3.9487 m. This is a sweep of separate static load cases, not a dynamic moving-load simulation.

Lecture 18

Introduction – Cable Support Systems

Setup and symbols.

A beam transmits a moment across its cut; an ideal flexible cable transmits only tangent tension. H is the positive horizontal tension component, T the nonnegative tension magnitude, and the segment’s tangent angle measured from positive x. The signed slope s = dy/dx uses y upward. At a downward point load P, are the slopes immediately left and right, both measured in the positive-x direction. They are not the directions of the two arrows on the isolated joint.

A flexible cable carries tension

An ideal perfectly flexible cable cannot transmit a bending couple or a compressive axial force. Its internal force is tangent to its current shape and pulls away from an isolated segment. Consequently, cable geometry is part of the equilibrium problem. A beam can resist bending while preserving an approximately prescribed shape; a cable must change direction so that its tensile forces can balance the loads.

If cable self-weight is neglected and loads are applied only at discrete points, each unloaded segment is straight. At a load point, adjacent segments generally have different directions and different tension magnitudes. If loading is continuously distributed, the cable shape is a curve. The correct curve depends on how the load is distributed: per horizontal distance or per actual cable length.

The constant horizontal component

Suppose all applied loads between supports are vertical. Isolate any cable segment. Horizontal equilibrium requires the horizontal tension component at its two ends to be equal in magnitude. Moving from segment to segment shows that one positive quantity H describes the horizontal component everywhere in the cable.

If a straight segment has slope s = rise divided by horizontal run, then its tension magnitude is

Thus tension magnitude is not generally constant, even though H is. The steepest segment has the largest tension for the same H. If a horizontal external force acts at an intermediate point, H can change across that point; the constant-H result relies on purely vertical intermediate loading.

A point load relates adjacent slopes

Take y positive upward and x positive right. Let the cable slopes immediately left and right of a downward point load P be sL and sR, both measured as y change per positive x change. The left segment pulls the joint left and with vertical component minus HsL. The right segment pulls right and with vertical component HsR. Vertical equilibrium gives

A downward load therefore increases the slope as we move from left to right. The left branch of a sagging cable has negative slope, the right branch positive slope, and the low point occurs where the sign changes or where the smooth slope is zero.

Worked example: a central load

Supports A and B are 8 m apart at the same elevation. A downward 12 kN load is attached at the midpoint, 2 m below the supports. Neglect cable weight. The left and right slopes are minus 0.5 and plus 0.5. Hence H times 1 equals 12 kN, so H = 12 kN. Each segment tension is

Each support supplies 6 kN upward to the cable and 12 kN outward horizontally. The cable pulls the supports downward and inward with opposite forces. State clearly whether a reported reaction acts on the cable or on the anchor.

Fig. 4.1 — Cable geometry with vertical concentrated loads. Each unloaded segment is straight; the dashed line is the support chord.

If the sag is reduced to 1 m, H doubles to 24 kN even though the vertical load remains 12 kN. This is the same shallow-angle amplification seen in trusses and toggles. A cable cannot support a transverse load while remaining perfectly straight with finite tension in this ideal model.

What information closes the problem

Support positions and loads do not always determine cable sag. One more geometric or mechanical specification is commonly needed: a sag value, a known point elevation, total cable length, or prescribed tension. Without it, a family of cable shapes can balance the same vertical loads with different horizontal components H.

The next lectures progress from one concentrated load to several, then to unequal supports and length constraints. The final lecture treats distributed suspension loads and distinguishes a parabola from a catenary.

A cable joint’s two tangent directions

Proposition: a downward point load increases the positive-x cable slope.

Under purely vertical intermediate loading, the common horizontal component H satisfies .

Fig. 4.2 — The two tangent forces pull away from the joint. Both slopes are defined toward increasing x, so the left force has components (−H, −HsL).

The right segment’s positive-x tangent is proportional to (1,sR). Its force on the joint is therefore (H,HsR). The left segment’s positive-x tangent is proportional to (1,sL), but that segment pulls the joint toward the left: its force is (−H,−HsL). Add those two vectors and the downward load (0,−P). Horizontal components cancel. Vertical balance is −HsL + HsR − P = 0, giving the result.

The same sign convention works when both slopes are negative. In that case the joint can be above one neighboring point and below the other; guessing “both tensions point upward” would fail. The coordinate derivation avoids that guess.

∎

Lecture 19

Cable Support Systems - Concentrated Loads

Setup and symbols.

Apply Lecture 18’s slope jump to one off-centre load. L is the support span, a and b its two horizontal load-point distances, f the downward sag below the equal-height support line, and S the geometric cable length. H is horizontal tension component; the two T values are segment magnitudes. A tension limit is a stipulated allowable magnitude in this exercise, not a measured strength or a complete design rule.

One load away from the centre

Let supports A and B have equal elevation and horizontal separation L. A downward point load P hangs at a horizontal distance a from A and b from B, with a + b = L. Its sag below the support line is f. The two segment slopes are minus f/a and plus f/b. Substituting into the slope-jump equation gives

The left support vertical reaction is Hf/a = Pb/L, and the right is Hf/b = Pa/L. These are the same vertical reactions as a simply supported beam with the same span and load location. The cable differs by also requiring horizontal reactions whose magnitude depends on sag.

Worked example: an offset hanging load

Fig. 4.3 — Cable geometry with vertical concentrated loads. Each unloaded segment is straight; the dashed line is the support chord.

Take L = 10 m, a = 4 m, b = 6 m, f = 2 m, and P = 15 kN. Then H = 18 kN. The left vertical reaction is 9 kN and the right is 6 kN. The tensions are

The shorter horizontal side is steeper because both sides rise by the same 2 m. It therefore has greater tension. At the load joint, the horizontal components cancel and the upward vertical components add to 15 kN. For the complete cable, the support moments also balance the applied load.

Reverse the question: allowable tension determines sag

Suppose the cable in the example must remain below an idealized tension limit of 25 kN. The steeper left segment controls. Its vertical component remains 9 kN for this equal-support, fixed-load geometry. Therefore,

Because H = 36/f with consistent kilonewton and metre units, the sag must satisfy f at least 36/23.324 = approximately 1.543 m. This is a statics-based minimum sag for the stated tension limit. It does not include a separate strength safety factor, anchor design, cable extension, or clearance constraints; those would be additional design inputs.

The inequality direction is important. Less sag requires more horizontal tension. A solution reporting a maximum sag from this tension constraint has reversed the physical trend.

Length and sag are linked

The total geometric length for one concentrated load is

If an inextensible cable's length is given, this equation determines f for the stated horizontal load position and equal support heights, after choosing the physically sagging branch. Once f is known, equilibrium determines H and the tensions. For the numerical example, S is approximately 10.797 m.

If cable stretch matters, geometric length and unstretched length are different. Tension then depends on both equilibrium and a constitutive relation for extension. Treating a substantially elastic cable as inextensible can mispredict sag and force, especially when the sag is small.

Why replacing the cable by one resultant is insufficient

The complete cable's force and moment equations find the vertical reaction split in the equal-height case, but horizontal equilibrium only says that the two horizontal reactions oppose each other. It does not determine their common magnitude. The cable's geometry provides the missing relation. This is an instructive example of equilibrium and geometry cooperating without invoking material stress analysis.

Back to module start

Lecture 20

Cable Support Systems - Concentrated Loads (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

One point load becomes several. is downward load i, applied at horizontal coordinate . The signed slopes immediately before and after it are . The horizontal component H is common only because the intermediate loads are vertical. In the cable–beam correspondence, is the moment of a simply supported reference beam and d(x) is positive cable sag below the support chord.

Editorial continuation: several point loads

For multiple vertical point loads, the cable is a polygon. Every unloaded span is straight, and every load point changes the slope according to H times the slope change equals the downward load. This offers a compact alternative to assigning a separate tension and angle to every segment.

Let load Pi act at xi. Write si for the slope of the segment just to its right and si-minus-one for the segment just to its left. Then

The support elevations impose a second geometric relation: the sum of each segment's slope times its horizontal length equals the total elevation change. A known intermediate elevation or sag then determines H.

Worked example: two equal loads and a flat middle segment

Supports A and B are at (0,0) and (12,0) m. Downward 6 kN loads act at x = 4 m and x = 8 m. Both load points lie 2 m below the supports. The three slopes are minus 0.5, zero, and plus 0.5. At either load, H times 0.5 equals 6 kN, so H = 12 kN.

The outer segment tensions are , and the middle segment tension is 12 kN. A horizontal cable segment can have nonzero tension. Its zero slope means zero vertical component, not zero axial force. Each support supplies 6 kN upward.

Worked example: unequal loads determine unequal elevations

Fig. 4.4 — Cable geometry with vertical concentrated loads. Each unloaded segment is straight; the dashed line is the support chord.

Keep the supports and horizontal load positions, but place 6 kN at x = 4 m and 9 kN at x = 8 m. Specify that the first load point has y = minus 2 m. Its first segment slope is minus 0.5. The subsequent slopes are

The supports have equal height, so the three 4 m segments must have slopes summing to zero:

Thus the middle slope is minus 1/14 and the last slope is 4/7. The second load point is at y = minus 2 minus 4/14 = minus 16/7 m, approximately minus 2.286 m. The second point is the lowest because the slope changes there from negative to positive.

The segment vertical components, measured in the positive-x direction, are minus 7, minus 1, and plus 8 kN. The corresponding tensions are

The support vertical reactions are 7 and 8 kN. Their sum is 15 kN, and moments about A give 8(12) = 6(4) + 9(8), a direct check.

The cable–beam correspondence

For equal-height supports and the same vertical load distribution, let Mb(x) be the bending moment of a simply supported reference beam. If d(x) is the cable's downward distance below the straight support chord, then

One way to derive this is to take moments about a cable point for the left cable portion. The vertical forces produce the same moment expression as the reference beam; the horizontal reaction supplies the balancing moment H times sag. This relation makes a cable's funicular shape proportional to a beam's moment diagram.

It does not mean the cable carries bending moment. It means the cable's shape allows axial tension to balance the moment that a straight beam would carry internally. This distinction links the beam and cable modules while preserving their different mechanical models.

Prove the cable–beam correspondence for unequal support heights

Proposition: sag below the chord satisfies Hd = Mᵦ.

Set the left support at (0,0), the right at (L,Δ), and let y(x) be the cable height. The straight chord is , and downward chord sag is . The reference beam has horizontal span L and the same vertical loads.

Fig. 4.5 — Computed unequal-support geometry A(0,0), C(4,−2), B(10,2) m. At C, the chord lies at y = 0.8 m, so downward chord sag is 2.8 m.

Let Ay and By be upward reactions on the actual cable. The right horizontal reaction is +H, so whole-cable moments give . If is the right reaction of the horizontal reference beam, then . Vertical force balance gives .

Take moments about a cable point at (x,y) for the portion to its left. The left support force is (−H,Ay), producing moment −xAy − yH. Each downward left-side load contributes . The tangent tension at the cut has no moment about the point. Hence

Substitute Ay and recognize the reference-beam moment:

Thus unequal support height changes the actual vertical reactions, but the reference-beam identity remains valid when sag is measured below the chord. Setting Δ = 0 recovers the equal-height result.

∎

Lecture 21

Cable Support Systems - Concentrated Loads (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

Lecture 20 used equal-height supports. We now distinguish vertical coordinate y from downward distance below the straight support chord. S is total geometric cable length, L horizontal span, f sag in the symmetric example, and the small excess length. The symbol marks an approximation whose neglected terms must be small; it is not an exact equilibrium equality.

Editorial continuation: unequal supports and a length constraint

Fig. 4.6 — Cable geometry with vertical concentrated loads. Each unloaded segment is straight; the dashed line is the support chord.

When supports have unequal elevations, horizontal reactions contribute to the whole-cable moment equation through the support-height difference. The vertical reactions are therefore not generally the same as those of a simple horizontal beam loaded at the same x coordinates. Begin with actual coordinates rather than importing the equal-height formulas.

Worked example: one load between unequal supports

Let A = (0,0) m, B = (10,2) m, and the load point C = (4,minus 2) m. A downward 15 kN force acts at C. The left slope is minus 2/4 = minus 0.5. The right slope is 4/6 = 2/3. Hence

The left vertical support force is H/2 = 45/7 kN, and the right is 2H/3 = 60/7 kN. They add to 15 kN. The tensions are approximately 14.375 kN on the left and 15.452 kN on the right. The right segment is now steeper despite having the larger horizontal run because it rises farther.

For the complete cable, the force at B is (H,60/7) kN. Its moment about A is

which balances the load moment 15(4). Omitting the horizontal force's 2 m lever arm would give the wrong vertical reaction.

Sag below the support chord

The straight chord joining A and B has equation y = 0.2x. At x = 4 m its elevation is 0.8 m, so the cable's distance below that chord is 2.8 m, not 2 m. The reference horizontal beam moment at that x is 36 kN m, and H times 2.8 equals 36. Thus the cable–beam correspondence still works when sag is measured below the support chord and the appropriate reference-beam construction is used.

The vertical coordinate and the chord sag answer different geometric questions. State which one is supplied before using a formula involving “sag.” Ambiguous sag definitions are a common source of apparently inconsistent cable calculations.

Worked example: prescribed cable length

Return to equal-height supports 10 m apart and a central point load of 12 kN. Suppose the cable is idealized as inextensible with total length 10.4 m. Symmetry makes each straight segment 5.2 m long and its horizontal projection 5 m. Pythagoras gives

The horizontal component is , and each tension is approximately 21.844 kN. The vertical component is 6 kN, providing an independent tension check through the right triangle of components.

Sensitivity near a taut configuration

If the cable length is only slightly greater than the support separation, the sag is small. Small errors in length can then create significant relative changes in sag and tension. In the symmetric point-load case, let the excess length be epsilon. Expanding the length formula for small f gives approximately

Because H is proportional to one over f, it grows roughly as one over the square root of the excess length. This sensitivity explains why installation tolerances, thermal expansion, and elastic stretch may matter strongly in nearly taut cables even if they seemed negligible in a generously sagging example.

For a general multi-load cable with prescribed total length, use the slope-jump equations and support geometry to express all segment lengths in terms of H, then solve the length equation. The remaining equation is usually nonlinear, but a numerical solution should still be checked against equilibrium and positive tensions.

Quantify the nearly taut limit

Proposition: central-load tension grows as the inverse square root of excess length near tautness.

Let an inextensible symmetric two-segment cable have span L, sag f, and length S = L + ε, with small positive ε/L.

Fig. 4.7 — Computed horizontal tension for a 10 m span and 12 kN central load as excess cable length varies. The exact curve and shallow approximation become close near zero excess length.

Square the exact length relation . It gives . Therefore the exact positive sag is . Neglecting ε² relative to 2Lε produces the shallow approximation.

The symbol ∼ means that the ratio of the two expressions approaches one in the stated limit. The relative sensitivity tends to : a 1% increase in small excess length produces approximately a 0.5% decrease in H. The exact derivative is supplied in the advanced exercise.

∎

Lecture 22

Cable Support Systems – Suspension Loads

Setup and symbols.

Replace discrete loads by a continuous load. w is downward force per horizontal length, while q is cable weight per actual cable length. H is horizontal tension component, x is horizontal distance from the lowest point, and y is height above it. A prime means differentiation with respect to x. The catenary length scale a = H/q has units of length. The functions and are hyperbolic cosine and sine.

Uniform per horizontal distance gives a parabola

Fig. 4.8 — Uniform vertical load per horizontal distance produces a parabolic cable. Uniform weight per cable length instead produces a catenary.

Consider a continuous flexible cable carrying downward load w per unit horizontal distance. This is an idealization of a suspension system where closely spaced vertical hangers transfer an approximately uniform deck load and cable self-weight is negligible by comparison. H remains constant because the distributed load has no horizontal component.

The vertical tension component is H times the cable slope y'. Over a short horizontal interval dx, its increase must balance w dx. Therefore,

If x = 0 is at the lowest point and y = 0 there, both integration constants vanish after imposing zero slope and zero elevation:

This is exactly parabolic within the stated ideal model; it does not require a small-slope approximation when loading is defined per horizontal distance and H is used correctly.

Equal supports and a specified sag

For equal-height supports separated by L, the lowest point is midway between them. Let f be the support elevation above that point. Substitution at x = L/2 gives

The smallest tension is H at the lowest point, where the slope is zero. The greatest tension occurs at the supports, where the slope magnitude is greatest. This conclusion is for the uniform vertical loading and equal supports specified here.

Worked example: a suspension load

Take L = 40 m, f = 4 m, and w = 5 kN/m of horizontal span. The total load is 200 kN and each vertical reaction is 100 kN. H = 250 kN, and the support tension is approximately 269.258 kN. At a point 10 m horizontally from the lowest point, y = 1 m, the slope is 0.2, and the tension is .

If the sag doubles while L and w remain unchanged, H halves. The support vertical component remains 100 kN, so the support tension does not halve exactly. This illustrates why it is useful to keep horizontal component and total tension separate.

Uniform cable self-weight gives a catenary

Now let q be the cable's weight per unit actual cable length. A small segment has length , so the vertical load per horizontal distance is q times that square root. The equilibrium equation becomes

Set a = H/q and p = y'. Separating variables gives . With zero slope at the lowest point, . Integrating again with y(0) = 0 yields

The length from the lowest point to coordinate x is . For equal supports, the total cable length is , and the sag is . A prescribed sag usually requires solving the latter equation for a numerically.

Worked catenary values and the shallow limit

Let a = 20 m, q = 1 kN/m of cable, and horizontal span L = 20 m. Then H = 20 kN. At each support x/a = 0.5, giving sag approximately 2.5525 m, support tension 22.5525 kN, and total cable length 20.8438 m. Each vertical support reaction is approximately 10.4219 kN, half the cable's weight.

For small x/a, the series for cosh gives . The catenary then resembles a parabola because cable length and horizontal length are nearly equal locally. The approximation should be judged from slope or x/a, not merely from the fact that the drawing looks shallow.

Choosing the load model

Before selecting either curve, ask what quantity is uniform. A uniform deck load per horizontal metre suggests the parabola. Uniform self-weight per cable metre suggests the catenary. Mixed deck load and cable weight generally require a combined equation. Discrete hangers produce a polygonal cable model unless a continuous approximation is justified by their spacing and the required accuracy.

This distinction is the central lesson of suspension loading: similar-looking curves can arise from different load measures, and the measure must appear correctly in the equilibrium equation.

Two load measures, two complete integrations

Proposition: uniform horizontal loading gives an exact parabola in the ideal flexible-cable model.

Let w be constant force per horizontal length, with origin at the lowest point.

Fig. 4.9 — Curves computed with H = 20 kN and densities w = q = 1 kN/m under their different length measures. Both have zero height and slope at the origin; the catenary rises farther away from it.

Vertical balance gives H y″ = w. Integrate once to obtain y′ = (w/H)x + c₁. The lowest-point slope y′(0) = 0 sets c₁ = 0. Integrate again: y = wx²/(2H) + c₂. Choosing y(0) = 0 sets c₂ = 0. At x = L/2, y = f, so . Solving for H produces . No small-slope approximation was made.

∎
Proposition: uniform cable self-weight gives a catenary.

Let q be constant force per actual cable length and define a = H/q.

The element’s length is , so vertical balance is . Set p = y′ and separate variables:

The antiderivative is arsinh u, the inverse hyperbolic sine, because differentiating arsinh u gives . Thus p = sinh(x/a). Integrating from the origin gives . The tangent-force components are H and Hp, so their magnitude is

Here cosh is positive, and the identity cosh² u − sinh² u = 1 follows directly from their exponential definitions. Integrating ds/dx = cosh(x/a) gives the half-length a sinh(x/a). Both the geometry and tension have now been derived from the same load measure.

∎

Fig. 4.10 — Prescribed sequence of separate static parabolic cable shapes for L = 20 m and w = 1 kN/m. The animation changes sag from 2 m to 4 m and back; H correspondingly changes from 25 kN to 12.5 kN. Animation time is not physical dynamics. A static comparison remains visible when reduced motion is requested.

Extension problems: load measure and inverse geometry

C4 · Two “uniform” loads that are different

Conceptual · Lecture 22 · Tests the meaning of load density

Fig. 4.11 — Curves computed with H = 20 kN and densities w = q = 1 kN/m under their different length measures. Both have zero height and slope at the origin; the catenary rises farther away from it.

Two cables have the same horizontal span and horizontal force component. One carries constant w per horizontal metre and the other constant q per cable metre, with w and q numerically equal. Which curve rises more rapidly away from the lowest point, and why?

Read the full solution

The catenary’s local horizontal load density is , which exceeds q wherever slope is nonzero. With the same H, its curvature y″ is larger. Algebraically, , whereas the parabola is only x²/(2a). Thus the catenary rises more rapidly away from the origin. Equal numerical densities are not equal loading distributions because the reference length differs.

D4 · Derive exact length sensitivity

Derivational · Lecture 21 · Tests logarithmic sensitivity

Fig. 4.12 — The exact geometric half-length S/2 is the hypotenuse of a triangle with horizontal leg L/2 and vertical leg f. This geometry supplies the length constraint before the tension is calculated.

For a symmetric central-load cable, derive H as a function of excess length ε = S − L, then compute .

Read the full solution

From and H = PL/(4f),

At fixed P and L, logarithmic differentiation gives

The limit is −1/2 as ε/L tends to zero. This dimensionless sensitivity is not the derivative dH/dε, whose units would be force per length.

K4 · Recover a catenary force from its sag

Computational investigation · Lecture 22 · Tests a nonlinear inverse problem

Fig. 4.13 — Computed sag as a function of the catenary length scale a for a 20 m span. Intersecting the curve with 2 m sag defines the inverse problem’s root.

A self-weight cable spans 20 m between equal-height supports, has sag 2 m, and weighs 1 kN per cable metre. Numerically solve for positive a. Report H, total length, and support tension. Compare H with the naive parabola result that treats q as a horizontal density.

Read the full solution

Define g(a) = a[cosh(10/a) − 1] − 2. It is positive at a = 20 m and negative at a = 30 m, so bisection brackets the root. Repeatedly replace the endpoint having the same sign as the midpoint until the sag error is below the desired tolerance. The computed result is 25.326487 m. Hence H = qa = 25.326487 kN, length is 20.523737 m, and support tension is 27.326487 kN.

The naive parabola gives H = 25 kN. The catenary value is larger because the cable-length load measure creates more load per horizontal metre on the sloping portions. Substituting the computed a back into g verifies the inverse solution independently of the reported force.

Lecture 23

Introduction – Coulomb Friction

Setup and symbols.

We now add a contact law to equilibrium. N is the compressive normal reaction; F is signed friction along the contact. Their units are force. and are dimensionless static and kinetic friction coefficients stipulated for a model. W is weight; R is the total contact resultant. The angle measures its tilt from the normal, and is the limiting friction angle. Coulomb friction is an empirical idealization, not a theorem derived from equilibrium.

Static friction is an adjustable force with a limit

A rough contact can transmit a normal compressive force N and a tangential friction force F. For the elementary Coulomb model of a sticking contact,

The dimensionless coefficient mu-s is the assumed static-friction coefficient for the contact condition. The inequality is fundamental. Below impending slip, friction takes the value needed for equilibrium, up to its limit. It is not automatically equal to mu-s times N.

If sliding occurs, the simplest kinetic model uses a magnitude opposing relative sliding. Real friction depends on materials, surface preparation, lubrication, speed, temperature, and history. The coefficients in this course's examples are stipulated model inputs, not measured data for a named material pair.

Worked example: a horizontal push

A block of weight 500 N rests on a horizontal floor with mu-s = 0.4. A horizontal 120 N force pushes it to the right. Vertical equilibrium gives N = 500 N. Horizontal equilibrium requires a 120 N friction force to the left. The capacity is 200 N, so the block can remain at rest. Setting friction equal to 200 N would create an unbalanced horizontal force and would contradict the assumed static state.

At a 200 N push, the block is at the ideal impending-slip limit. At a 240 N push, no sticking equilibrium exists under the model. If mu-k = 0.3 and the block slides right, friction is 150 N left. Its subsequent acceleration belongs to dynamics; a static solution cannot be rescued by pretending the kinetic friction somehow rises to 240 N.

Fig. 5.1 — Forces on the block. Normal and friction act at the floor; the normal resultant reaches the forward edge at impending tipping.

Direction follows relative motion or its tendency

Static friction opposes the local tendency for relative slip, not necessarily the externally applied force and not necessarily the overall motion of a larger machine. A driven wheel can experience forward friction from the ground. In a wedge assembly, different contacts can have different slip directions. When the direction is uncertain, assign a signed tangential force and solve equilibrium before checking its magnitude and interpreting its sign.

The friction angle

The contact resultant R combines N and F. If phi is the angle between R and the contact normal, then

At impending slip, the resultant lies on the boundary of this admissible angular region. In three dimensions the analogous set is a friction cone around the normal. In a plane it appears as two limiting rays. The construction is useful for graphical reasoning, but its algebraic content is still the same inequality.

A contact can open

The condition N at least zero means an ordinary surface can push but cannot pull. If equilibrium requires negative N, the assumed contact is not active. A friction force at that contact cannot remain available after separation. This couples normal and tangential feasibility: friction capacity vanishes when the normal contact force vanishes in the elementary model.

Distributed contact and rigid-body equilibrium

A block rests on a finite patch, not literally a point. The resultant normal force can shift within that patch to balance moments. If its required location reaches an edge, tipping may occur before sliding. The first lecture isolates the basic force law; later lectures add incline geometry, tipping, ladders, wedges, and multiple contacts. In every case, start with equilibrium and then test the contact conditions.

Lecture 24

Coulomb Friction (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

Use the friction inequality from Lecture 23 in axes adapted to the contact. W is block weight, incline angle, and P the applied uphill force. F is positive uphill in the incline equations. In the separate horizontal-floor example, is the pull angle above horizontal. The normal N must remain nonnegative, and the analysis assumes tipping has been excluded or checked separately.

Editorial continuation: inclined planes and oblique pulls

Choose axes parallel and normal to the contact surface. A block of weight W on an incline of angle alpha has a downslope weight component W sin alpha and a normal component W cos alpha. With no other applied force, equilibrium requires upslope friction equal to W sin alpha and normal force equal to W cos alpha. Rest is possible if

The limiting angle is the friction angle. Weight cancels because both the tangential demand and normal capacity scale with W in this simple model.

Worked example: the full range of an upslope force

Fig. 5.2 — Inclined-block force geometry. The illustrated friction arrow points downhill; the algebra must determine its actual sign for the specified P.

A block weighs 1000 N on a 20-degree incline. A force P acts parallel to the plane uphill, and mu-s = 0.4. The normal force is 1000 cos 20 degrees = 939.693 N, so the friction limit is 375.877 N. Let F be positive uphill. Along the plane,

Applying the friction inequality gives

Numerically, minus 33.857 N is the lower bound and 717.897 N is the upper bound. If P is constrained to be a nonnegative pulling force, the feasible range is 0 through 717.897 N. For P less than 342.020 N, friction acts uphill. For P greater than that value, friction acts downhill. At exactly 342.020 N, friction is zero. A single contact changes friction direction as the applied force changes, while remaining stationary throughout the interior range.

An upward pull reduces normal force

On a horizontal floor, let P pull at angle beta above horizontal. For a block of weight W,

at impending rightward sliding, with friction left. The threshold is

This expression assumes contact is maintained and tipping is excluded or checked separately. A downward push at the same acute angle changes the sign of the vertical component, increases N, and uses a denominator cos beta minus mu-s sin beta when the corresponding sliding equation is admissible.

Worked example: choosing a pull angle

For W = 500 N, mu-s = 0.4, and beta = 30 degrees, the threshold is approximately 187.61 N. The normal force at that threshold is approximately 406.19 N. A horizontal pull would require 200 N, so the upward component has reduced the force needed for sliding.

If beta is freely selectable and tipping is ignored, minimize P by maximizing its denominator. Differentiating cos beta plus mu-s sin beta gives minus sin beta plus mu-s cos beta. Setting this to zero yields

For this example, the optimum is about 21.80 degrees and the minimum force about 185.70 N. This optimum belongs to the stated point-force, sliding-only model. The pull's application height and the block dimensions may cause tipping first, which the next lecture examines.

Solve the state, not just a threshold formula

A question asking whether a block rests under a given force is different from asking for the force that starts motion. For the first, solve the required F and N and test the inequality. For the second, propose a limiting mode and use equality, then verify all other contacts and failure modes. The distinction prevents a large fraction of friction errors.

Prove the optimum and check contact

Proposition: the minimum sliding-only pull occurs at the friction angle.

On a level floor with fixed , allow pull angle , neglect tipping, and retain compressive contact.

Fig. 5.3 — Computed sliding-only threshold for a 500 N block with μs = 0.4. The minimum lies at β = arctan(0.4); tipping is a separate constraint.

The denominator of the threshold is D = cos β + μs sin β. By the angle-addition formula, , where tan φs = μs. Cosine is at most one, so D is maximized at β = φs. Since the numerator μsW is fixed and nonnegative, that maximizes the denominator and minimizes P.

The optimum therefore preserves compressive contact. Its tipping admissibility still depends on the force application point and block dimensions; this calculation has not established those.

Lecture 25

Coulomb Friction (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

A feasible friction force does not alone guarantee that a finite block stays upright. W is weight, b base width in the push direction, h horizontal-push height, P push magnitude, and e the forward shift of the normal resultant from the base centre. N is total normal reaction, not local pressure. The subscripts “tip” and “slide” label two different limiting values of P.

Editorial continuation: sliding versus tipping

A finite block can lose equilibrium in two different ways. The tangential force demand can exceed friction capacity, causing sliding. Or the required normal-reaction line can move outside the base, causing tipping. The first depends strongly on friction coefficient; the second depends on geometry and force application height. Both must be checked before naming the onset mode.

Let a rectangular block have base width b in the push direction and weight W acting through its centred mass centre. A horizontal force P pushes right at height h above the floor. Let e be the horizontal shift of the normal resultant from the base midpoint toward the right edge. Vertical equilibrium gives N = W. Moment equilibrium about the base midpoint gives

The contact pressure must remain compressive within the footprint, so the resultant cannot lie beyond the edge: e is at most b/2. At impending tipping,

The sliding limit is . The smaller threshold occurs first, provided the other equilibrium conditions hold at that threshold.

Worked example: a tall block

Fig. 5.4 — Forces on the block. Normal and friction act at the floor; the normal resultant reaches the forward edge at impending tipping.

Let W = 800 N, b = 0.6 m, and h = 1.2 m. The tipping threshold is 200 N. If mu-s = 0.4, the sliding threshold is 320 N, so tipping occurs first. At P = 200 N the required friction is only 200 N, below its 320 N limit, while the normal resultant has reached the right edge.

If the same floor has mu-s = 0.15, the sliding threshold is 120 N. At that force, e = 120(1.2)/800 = 0.18 m, still inside the 0.3 m half-width. Sliding occurs first. Increasing friction can therefore change the failure mode from sliding to tipping without making the block unconditionally safer against every motion.

Geometric criterion for the first mode

Compare the two formulas. Tipping precedes sliding when

If equality holds, the ideal model reaches both limits simultaneously. A small change in geometry, coefficient, or load direction may decide which motion develops. The criterion assumes a horizontal push, a centred weight, and a level base. It should not be applied unchanged to an oblique force or an off-centre mass centre.

Why moments about the edge are useful

At impending tipping, the contact resultant passes through the pivot edge. Taking moments about that edge eliminates the unknown normal and friction forces because their lines meet there in the ideal point-contact limit. The equation becomes P times h equals W times b/2. This gives the same threshold with less algebra.

Before tipping, however, the normal resultant is not known to act at that edge. Placing it there for every load artificially forces the block into a limiting state. The unknown reaction location is part of the ordinary sticking equilibrium problem.

Contact pressure and what statics does not determine

Rigid-body equilibrium determines the total normal force and its resultant location. It generally does not determine the detailed pressure distribution across the base. That distribution depends on compliance and geometry. One can nevertheless reject a solution requiring the resultant outside the support footprint because no nonnegative pressure distribution over that footprint can produce it.

This is another example of feasibility reasoning: equilibrium produces a required contact action, and geometry plus the contact law determine whether that action is possible. The same logic will organize the ladder and wedge examples.

Why the normal resultant must stay within the footprint

Proposition: nonnegative contact pressure bounds the reaction location.

Use coordinate ξ across the base, with −b/2 ≤ ξ ≤ b/2. Let p(ξ) be nonnegative normal force per base length, integrated across the out-of-page width if necessary.

Fig. 5.5 — The normal resultant N must lie inside the base footprint. Its offset e balances the horizontal push moment; p(ξ) denotes the distributed nonnegative contact pressure resultant per unit base length, not a computed pressure profile.

The total normal is , and its location is , for N > 0. Since every ξ in the loaded footprint lies between −b/2 and b/2, multiply these bounds by nonnegative p and integrate. Dividing by N gives . Moment equilibrium independently requires e = Ph/W. At e = b/2 the normal action has reached the forward edge; a larger e cannot be supplied by any compressive pressure distribution over that base.

This proves the admissibility bound without assuming a uniform or linear pressure distribution. The actual distribution requires a deformation model.

Lecture 26

Coulomb Friction (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

Combine moment balance with two contacts. L is ladder length, W ladder weight, its angle to the floor, R the smooth wall’s horizontal reaction, N the floor normal, and F the floor friction. A person has weight Q and position s measured along the ladder from its foot. The distance s is not horizontal; its moment arm for a vertical force is .

Editorial continuation: a ladder with two contacts

A ladder makes the interaction between force balance, moment balance, and friction particularly clear. Model a uniform ladder of length L and weight W resting on a rough horizontal floor and leaning against a smooth vertical wall. Its angle above the floor is theta. The wall supplies only a horizontal normal force R. The floor supplies an upward normal N and horizontal friction F. Neglect ladder thickness and assume a rigid ladder.

The ladder would tend to have its top slide down the wall and its foot slide away from the wall. Floor friction therefore acts toward the wall. Vertical equilibrium gives N = W, and horizontal equilibrium gives F = R. Moments about the foot eliminate both floor forces:

The required coefficient is therefore

Worked example: ladder alone

Fig. 5.6 — Ladder free-body diagram. The wall pushes left; floor friction acts toward the wall. Weight acts at the midpoint for a uniform ladder.

For W = 200 N and theta = 60 degrees, R and F are approximately 57.735 N. The floor normal is 200 N, so the minimum coefficient is approximately 0.2887. If mu-s = 0.4, the friction demand is below the 80 N capacity. No equality should be imposed at the floor unless the problem is specifically asking for a limiting condition.

Worked example: a person climbs the ladder

Now a person of weight Q stands a distance s along the ladder from the foot. Vertical equilibrium gives N = W + Q. Taking moments about the foot gives

At impending sliding, set R equal to mu-s times (W + Q). Solving for the permitted position gives

Use W = 200 N, Q = 800 N, L = 5 m, theta = 60 degrees, and mu-s = 0.4. Then s-max is approximately 3.705 m along the ladder. If the expression exceeded L, the entire ladder length would satisfy this particular slip check. If it were negative, the modeled system would fail the slip condition even with the person at the foot.

Why roughness at the wall changes the problem

A rough wall can also exert vertical friction. Then vertical equilibrium becomes N plus wall friction equals total weight, and the wall friction also affects the moment balance depending on the selected moment centre. There are more contact unknowns. Static friction laws are inequalities, so the interior equilibrium may not be uniquely determined by rigid-body statics alone.

It is generally incorrect to set both contacts to their friction limits merely because both are rough. A stated impending motion may justify a particular limiting combination, but it must be checked for consistent slip directions and feasible normal forces. Otherwise, determine a feasible range or use additional contact/compliance information rather than inventing an equality at every surface.

Reading the geometry correctly

The person distance s is measured along the ladder, so its horizontal moment arm about the foot is s cos theta. The wall normal's vertical lever arm is L sin theta. Mixing these projections produces an erroneous tangent instead of cotangent, or vice versa. Draw the force line and its perpendicular distance before simplifying trigonometry.

This ladder is a teaching model for equilibrium, not a field-use ladder rating. Its value here is that every force direction, moment arm, and inequality can be traced to a stated assumption.
