Lecture 27

Coulomb Friction (cont.)

Setup and symbols.

The wedge extends the interacting-body analysis to a slipping contact. W is guided-block weight, P the horizontal wedge input, top-surface angle above horizontal, N the upper-contact normal, and the stated limiting coefficient at that contact. Write . The floor and vertical guide are smooth. Friction direction follows the block’s motion relative to the wedge, which differs from the wedge’s motion relative to the floor.

Editorial continuation: wedges and interacting rough bodies

A wedge converts horizontal motion into vertical motion. Its sloping contact creates a large normal force, and friction changes both the required input and whether a load can drive the wedge backward. The main difficulty is keeping the contact forces opposite on the two bodies and assigning friction from their relative slip, not from the absolute direction of the applied input.

Consider a block constrained by a smooth vertical guide so it can move only vertically. A wedge beneath it rests on a smooth horizontal floor. The wedge's top rises to the right at angle alpha. The wedge is driven left by a horizontal force P, lifting the block. The upper contact has coefficient mu, the block weight is W, and the wedge weight is neglected for this example.

Derive the lifting force from the block diagram

Fig. 5.7 — Schematic of the guided-block wedge. Upper-contact friction on the rising block acts down the slope; the smooth guide supplies horizontal balance.

As the wedge moves left, the block moves up relative to the wedge along the inclined surface toward the right. Friction on the block therefore acts down the incline, left and downward. Let N be the normal magnitude. The normal on the block points up and left. At impending upward relative sliding, its vertical components give

The block's vertical guide balances the horizontal force and supplies no vertical force. The force of the block on the wedge is opposite: its horizontal component is rightward with magnitude N sin alpha plus mu N cos alpha. Since the floor is smooth, the leftward input must balance that component:

where phi = arctan mu. The denominator must be positive for the assumed finite lifting equilibrium. Additional floor friction would add a different contact force and alter this result.

Worked example: lifting a guided load

Let W = 2000 N, alpha = 10 degrees, and mu = 0.2. Then N is approximately 2105.1 N and P approximately 780.2 N. With zero contact friction, the required input would be W tan 10 degrees, approximately 352.7 N. Friction has more than doubled the input in this particular shallow-wedge example.

The wedge's floor normal is 2000 N because its top contact receives the full downward load and the floor is horizontal. The vertical guide carries the block's horizontal balance. Omitting that guide reaction would leave the block unable to remain on its prescribed vertical path.

Lowering reverses the contact friction

If the wedge moves right and the block lowers, the block's relative motion along the top is down the incline to the left. Friction on the block is now up the incline. Its normal equation becomes N(cos alpha plus mu sin alpha) = W. The horizontal force of the block on the wedge is proportional to

If alpha is greater than phi, this force can drive the wedge rightward and a leftward holding force is needed at the lowering limit. If alpha is less than phi, the expression is negative: the load alone does not drive the wedge out under this ideal model, and a rightward extraction force is required. This is self-locking.

For alpha = 10 degrees and mu = 0.2, phi is approximately 11.31 degrees. The wedge is self-locking in the stated model, with an ideal limiting rightward extraction force about 45.7 N. This conclusion changes if the contact coefficient, guide arrangement, or floor roughness changes.

A general method for multiple contacts

Draw each body separately. Define a tangent and a normal at every contact. Draw action-reaction pairs consistently. Propose the impending relative motion and assign limiting friction accordingly. Solve force and moment equilibrium. Then check normal positivity, unused friction inequalities, and any tipping conditions. If a check fails, revise the assumed contact state rather than retaining an impossible force solution.

This procedure is longer than memorizing a wedge formula, but it transfers to screws, clamps, brakes, and other mechanisms whose contact geometry differs from the textbook sketch.

Check relative motion before choosing friction

Proposition: a left-moving rising-to-the-right wedge lifts a vertically guided block, which moves uphill relative to the wedge.

Let X be the wedge’s horizontal translation, positive right. Its top has equation , where c fixes the reference height. The guide fixes the block’s x coordinate.

Fig. 5.8 — The wedge surface moves left while a fixed horizontal guide coordinate forces the block upward. The relative velocity is uphill, so limiting friction on the block is downhill.

Differentiate the contact-height equation at fixed block x: . For a left-moving wedge, , so the block rises. Its velocity relative to the wedge has components , directed uphill along the surface. Friction on the block opposes this relative motion and acts downhill. Reversing wedge motion reverses that relative tangent direction and hence the limiting friction direction.

The dots denote time derivatives used only to identify a compatible motion direction. The force analysis remains quasi-static; no inertial term has been introduced.

Lecture 28

Belt Friction

Setup and symbols.

We integrate local Coulomb friction around a curved contact. is accumulated contact angle in radians. T is tension at a position along the belt; dT is its small increase toward the tight side. dN is the small normal contact force on a short element. are the positive end tensions sorted by magnitude. The exponential uses the dimensionless product . This model neglects belt weight, bending stiffness, and speed-related inertia.

Friction can accumulate around a curved surface

A flexible belt or rope wrapped around a rough cylinder can sustain different tensions at its two ends. The larger tension side is called the tight side and the smaller the slack side. The rope's curvature creates normal contact force; friction associated with that normal force permits tension to change along the wrap.

Assume a flexible belt of negligible weight and bending stiffness, a fixed cylindrical surface, continuous contact, a constant friction coefficient, and impending gross slip. Let theta be the total contact angle in radians. We will derive the limiting tension ratio rather than treat it as a formula to memorize.

Equilibrium of a small belt element

Isolate a short element spanning angle dtheta. Let its tensions be T and T + dT. To first order, the radial components of the endpoint tensions require a normal contact magnitude

At impending slip, the tangential friction magnitude is mu-s dN. Choose the direction of increasing theta from the lower-tension side toward the higher-tension side. Tangential equilibrium then gives

Separate variables and integrate across the contact:

This is the capstan equation. Cylinder radius cancels because the normal demand depends on the change of direction. Radius still matters for the torque produced by a given tension difference.

Fig. 5.9 — A flexible rope over a fixed drum with a half-wrap. A support torque balances the unequal endpoint tensions.

Below the slipping limit

If the belt is sticking and both tensions are positive, the condition is

As with block friction, equality belongs to a limiting state. The coefficient and wrap angle specify a capacity, not the actual tension ratio in every static configuration. Actual tensions also depend on loads, torque balance, and how the belt is installed or held.

Worked example: a half-wrap

A rope wraps halfway around a fixed cylinder, so theta = pi radians. Let mu-s = 0.3 and the held low-side tension be 100 N. The maximum high-side tension without slip is

If the actual high-side load is 220 N, the ratio 2.2 is below the limiting ratio about 2.566. The rope can remain stuck under the ideal assumptions, and the actual friction is below its fully mobilized limiting distribution. If the load is 300 N, the assumed 100 N holding force is insufficient.

Radians are not optional

The differential derivation uses the small-angle relation with angle measured in radians. Substituting 180 into the exponent for a half-wrap would produce a meaningless enormous ratio. Convert degrees using theta-radians = theta-degrees times pi/180 before calculating. The exponent must be dimensionless, as must a tension ratio.

What the elementary formula leaves out

A rapidly moving belt can require centrifugal effects. A belt with significant stiffness may not conform ideally to a small pulley. Nonuniform contact conditions can require integrating a varying coefficient over angle. A grooved V-belt has a different normal-force relationship because of the groove geometry. Those cases should not be forced into the flat, massless, fixed-cylinder derivation without modification.

The essential idea is local Coulomb friction integrated along a curved contact. It explains the exponential dependence on wrap angle and connects the last topic of the syllabus directly to the first friction inequality.

Keep the finite-angle terms until their order is clear

Proposition: the limiting capstan ratio follows from local equilibrium to first order.

Take a short element of angular width Δθ, with endpoint tensions T and T + ΔT. Use axes tangent and inward-normal to its midpoint.

Fig. 5.10 — The isolated short rope element has two endpoint tensions directed away from it. Their inward components create the normal contact requirement; tangent friction balances their small difference.

The inward components of the two endpoint tensions add to . The surface pushes outward with equal magnitude ΔN. Since sin(Δθ/2) = Δθ/2 plus terms of third order, and ΔT itself is first order in Δθ, the leading normal balance is ΔN = T Δθ. The tangential imbalance is ΔT cos(Δθ/2), whose leading term is ΔT. At impending slip, tangential friction is μs ΔN. Dividing by Δθ and taking the limit gives dT/dθ = μsT.

Integrating dT/T from the low side to the high side gives ln(Thigh/Tlow) = μsθ and hence the exponential ratio. In sticking contact, replace equality locally by the bound on tangential traction, producing the logarithmic inequality. This inequality is the aggregate capacity of the ideal model, not a prescribed friction distribution for every installation.

∎

Lecture 29

Belt Friction - Examples

Setup and symbols.

Lecture 28 supplied a limiting ratio; these examples add torque and installation constraints. r is pulley radius, torque magnitude, and the dimensionless limiting tension ratio. This k is unrelated to the beam-load gradient in Lecture 17. A specified tension sum is additional information; it is not implied by the capstan equation. The natural logarithm is the inverse of the exponential.

Example 1: how much wrap is needed?

A fixed drum must allow a 100 N holding tension to restrain a 1000 N load. Assume mu-s = 0.25 and negligible rope weight. At the minimum wrap, the tension ratio is at its limit. Solving the capstan equation for angle gives

Dividing by 2pi gives approximately 1.466 turns of contact. This is the ideal mathematical threshold, not an added engineering margin. The logarithm matters: doubling the desired ratio does not double the required angle, but adds ln 2 divided by mu-s.

Example 2: torque capacity of a belt contact

Let a pulley of radius r = 0.15 m be acted on tangentially by a belt with low-side tension 200 N. The contact angle is pi radians and mu-s = 0.3. At impending slip the high-side tension is approximately 513.27 N. The torque magnitude supplied by the belt is

The tension difference produces torque; the tension sum contributes strongly to bearing loading, with the exact bearing resultant depending on the directions of the two free belt spans. Do not use the tension sum in the torque formula. Nor should you infer the bearing load from the difference alone.

Example 3: prescribed total tension

An ideal belt installation is specified to have during the loading considered. Let r = 0.2 m, theta = pi, and mu-s = 0.25. The prescribed sum is an additional assumption; statics and the capstan inequality do not supply it automatically.

At the slip limit, define k = exp(mu-s theta), approximately 2.19328. Then T-high = k T-low and

The limiting torque is approximately 74.74 N m. A real belt's pretension and elastic stretching determine how its total tension evolves; the constant-sum condition is a stated simplified model, not a universal property.

Example 4: a drum that is free to rotate

The fixed-cylinder assumption is easy to overlook. Suppose a rope contacts an ideal pulley on a frictionless axle, with no applied holding torque and negligible rotational inertia in static equilibrium. Taking moments of the pulley requires equal tensions on its two tangential sides. Contact friction alone does not permit an arbitrary unequal-tension static state if the pulley itself is free to rotate and has no torque balance.

The capstan inequality can still describe what the contact could sustain, but the pulley equilibrium supplies an additional restriction. For a fixed capstan, the support provides the balancing torque. For a freely rotating ideal pulley, it does not. This example shows why analyzing only the rope can miss an essential body in the system.

Example 5: infer the required coefficient

A fixed contact has wrap angle 210 degrees and must sustain a tension ratio of 3. Convert the angle to 7pi/6 radians. The minimum model coefficient is

This is a requirement inferred from the model. It is not evidence that a particular rope and drum actually have that coefficient. Measured behavior under the intended conditions is a separate input.

A belt-friction solution checklist in prose

Identify which object is fixed and where the balancing torque comes from. Mark the actual contact angle, not the angle between the free spans unless geometry proves they coincide. Determine the intended slip direction, hence which side is tight. Use equality only for a limiting question. Convert angle to radians, solve the ratio, and combine it with any separate force or torque constraints. Finally, verify that both tensions remain positive and that the required reaction torque has somewhere to go.

Lecture 30

Course Wrap-up

Setup and symbols.

The final synthesis connects earlier models. P is a downward load, L the supported span, f the cable sag, and H its horizontal tension component. In the worked beam-and-drum system, T is cable tension, the lower end tension, and the drum-contact coefficient. Each model supplies one part of the solution; no single equilibrium result establishes both material capacity and contact feasibility.

One method, several mechanical models

The course has repeatedly used the same laws: force balance, moment balance, and action-reaction. What changes from topic to topic is the admissible interaction. A truss bar acts along its axis. A frame joint can pass two planar force components. A beam section transmits a force and a moment. A cable pulls tangentially and changes shape. A rough contact supports only certain combinations of normal and tangential force.

This suggests a powerful order for solving new problems. First identify the mechanical model. Then choose a body or cut that exposes the desired unknown. Only after that choose equations. Beginning with a familiar formula before identifying the model is how a cable gets assigned compression, a roller gets assigned a couple, or static friction gets incorrectly fixed at its maximum.

A unifying example: the same span, two different structures

A simply supported beam of span L carries a central point load P. Its reactions are P/2 and its maximum bending moment is PL/4. A weightless cable between equal-height supports carries the same central load with sag f. Its vertical reactions are also P/2, but its horizontal component is

The relation Hf = PL/4 connects the cable's sag to the beam's central moment. The beam resists the loading through internal bending; the cable uses geometric sag and horizontal thrust. Similar external loads do not imply similar internal force mechanisms or support requirements.

Four different kinds of limitation

A determinate equilibrium problem has enough independent equations to solve its force unknowns. A stable arrangement has the necessary geometric restraint. An admissible contact solution respects tension-only or friction restrictions. A strong-enough design has adequate material and connection capacity. These are distinct requirements. Passing one does not automatically pass the others.

For example, an overhanging beam can have a unique algebraic reaction solution that demands uplift at an unanchored support. A compressed truss member can have a valid equilibrium force but buckle under it. A symmetric spatial joint can balance one vertical load while lacking lateral restraint. Keeping these distinctions explicit is a mark of mature engineering reasoning.

A final worked synthesis

A 4 m beam is pinned at its left end. Its right end is supported by a cable running upward and left at 30 degrees above horizontal. A downward 6 kN load acts at the beam's midpoint. Moment equilibrium about the pin requires the cable's upward component to be 3 kN, so its tension is 6 kN. The pin supplies 3 kN upward and approximately 5.196 kN rightward.

Suppose the cable's other end wraps pi radians around a fixed rough drum with mu-s = 0.3 and is held by a lower tension. The minimum holding tension at impending slip is

The beam's maximum bending moment is 6 kN m at midspan. The horizontal cable component also places the beam in compression with magnitude approximately 5.196 kN. A later strength calculation would need both effects, not just bending. The drum support must sustain the torque caused by the two cable tensions, so it must not be modeled as a free ideal pulley.

This one system combines rigid-body reactions, beam cuts, cable direction, friction capacity, and a support-torque requirement. Each subsystem is simple once isolated correctly. The skill is to connect them without losing an interaction at a boundary.

Where to go next

Mechanics of materials explains how axial force, shear, bending, and torsion create stress and deformation. Structural analysis adds compatibility and stiffness to solve indeterminate structures. Dynamics restores inertia for moving mechanisms. Stability and buckling explain why an equilibrium configuration may fail under a small disturbance. Contact mechanics refines the rigid Coulomb model when pressure distributions and deformation matter.

For a computational extension, implement a small truss equilibrium solver that accepts joint coordinates and member connectivity. Have it report residuals, rank, and tension/compression signs, not just a force vector. Then deliberately introduce a mechanism or a tension-only member with a negative solution. A useful solver should expose those modeling failures rather than hide them behind a successful numerical solve.

The final assessment asks you to reconstruct these ideas on new numbers. Treat a correct free-body diagram and an explicit admissibility check as part of the answer, not as optional decoration around the arithmetic.

Equilibrium determines demand; the coefficient determines its upper bound.

Read the full solution

The normal force is 600 N. Actual friction is 150 N opposite the push; its limiting magnitude is 180 N. Sticking is possible because 150 is less than 180. The unused 30 N is a margin in this ideal force model, not an extra friction force acting on the block.

Problem 2

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

The block has a 0.4 m base and is pushed at height 1 m. With the same weight and coefficient, does it slide or tip first?

Open a hint

Compare two distinct limiting loads.

Read the full solution

, while . It tips first. At tipping the friction demand 120 N is feasible. Thus the 150 N sticking conclusion in the previous point-mass-style sliding check would not describe this finite block with the newly specified high push point.

Problem 1

Foundation problem · Apply the model, show the equations, then check feasibility.

A 400 N block is pulled horizontally with 100 N on a surface with mu-s = 0.3. Find friction and its limit.

Actual friction is 100 N opposite the pull. The normal force is 400 N and the limit is 120 N. The sliding condition permits rest; finite-block tipping must be checked separately if dimensions and force height matter.

The wall reaction and floor friction are . The floor normal is 300 N, so the minimum coefficient is 0.5.

. The equality represents impending slip. Greater holding tension can keep the same load within the sticking range, subject to the opposite-slip limit as well.

Problem 1

Read the full solution

, giving T = 7.5 kN. The cable force is (−4.5,6) kN; the pin supplies (4.5,4) kN. Shear is 4 kN before x = 3 m and −6 kN after it. The moment peaks at 12 kN m under the point load, and returns to zero at x = 5 m. The beam also carries 4.5 kN compression. All three force components and the moment balance close.

Extension problems: contact states and capacity

C5 · Why two rough contacts need not both be at their limits

Conceptual · Lectures 23 and 26 · Tests inequality constraints

Fig. 5.11 — A rough wall and rough floor supply separate normal and tangential reactions. The arrows show a candidate slip-resisting state; neither friction magnitude is automatically at its limit.

A ladder rests between a rough floor and a rough wall. A proposed solution sets friction equal to μN at both contacts merely because both surfaces are rough. Identify the unsupported assumption and describe a better analysis.

Read the full solution

Roughness supplies bounds, not equalities in every equilibrium state. Simultaneous equality assumes both contacts are at limiting friction in directions compatible with one proposed motion. Start with separate signed tangential forces, nonnegative normals, and the three rigid-body equilibrium equations. Apply both friction inequalities. This may define a feasible range rather than a unique force distribution. If studying impending motion, specify the mode and test the other contact constraints after solving it.

D5 · Torque capacity with a fixed tension sum

Derivational · Lecture 29 · Tests a coupled constraint

Fig. 5.12 — Both tangent tension lines lie a perpendicular distance r from the pulley axis. Their moments oppose, so the net magnitude is r times the tension difference, even when their sum S is fixed.

Assume a fixed positive tension sum S, pulley radius r, and limiting ratio . Derive the maximum torque in terms of S, r, and k. Then find its limits as friction-angle product tends to zero or becomes large.

Read the full solution

The limiting equations are Thigh = kTlow and Thigh + Tlow = S. Therefore Tlow = S/(k+1), Thigh = kS/(k+1), and

The hyperbolic tangent is defined by tanh u = (exp(2u) − 1)/(exp(2u) + 1), so the last equality is algebraic. At zero μsθ, the tensions must match and torque vanishes. At large μsθ, torque approaches rS, not infinity, because the total tension is fixed. This saturation would be missed by varying the ratio while holding the low-side tension fixed instead.

K5 · Find the coefficient at which the first failure mode switches

Computational investigation · Lecture 25 · Tests a regime boundary

Fig. 5.13 — Computed first-motion boundary for W = 900 N, base b = 0.6 m, and push height h = 0.9 m. The first threshold follows sliding below μs = 1/3 and tipping above it.

A block weighs 900 N, has base width 0.6 m, and is pushed horizontally at height 0.9 m. Sweep μs from 0.1 to 0.6. Plot the first-motion threshold and identify the mode switch. What changes at the threshold coefficient?

Read the full solution

The sliding limit is 900μs N, while tipping is fixed at 300 N. Thus the first threshold is N and the switch occurs at μs = 1/3. Below that value sliding occurs first; above it tipping occurs first. At equality the ideal model reaches the friction limit and edge-resultant condition simultaneously. At μs = 0.1 the threshold is 90 N, at 0.3 it is 270 N, and at 0.6 it remains 300 N. More friction does not raise the tipping threshold.

Model register: what each idealization captures and misses

Use this register after the main derivations. It separates a force demand that equilibrium can determine from additional questions about deformation, stability, and contact. A model’s omissions are not interchangeable: adding friction will not supply a missing elastic compatibility equation.

ModelWhat it determines hereWhat it omits and where to go next
Rigid body and ideal pinNet forces, moments, and pin interactions in Lectures 2–5.Pin clearance, bearing stress, and flexibility. Mechanics of materials is needed for local stress and displacement.
Two-force truss barAxial demands from joint and section equilibrium in Lectures 6–13.Transverse loading, eccentric joints, elastic compatibility, and buckling. Lecture 13 identifies the extension law; a stiffness or stability analysis is the next step.
Beam section resultantsAxial force, shear, and bending moment versus position in Lectures 14–17.Stress distribution and deflection. These require cross-sectional geometry, constitutive data, and compatibility.
Perfectly flexible cableTension and compatible shape in Lectures 18–22.Bending stiffness, elastic stretch, and dynamic vibration. Lecture 21 discusses length sensitivity; an elastic-cable model must add force-dependent extension.
Coulomb contactAdmissible tangential force and limiting slip in Lectures 23–27.Detailed pressure, microslip, wear, temperature effects, and deformation-dependent friction. Lecture 25 derives a resultant-location bound without pretending to know the pressure field.
Massless flexible beltStatic tension-ratio capacity in Lectures 28–29.Centrifugal effects, bending stiffness, groove geometry, and installation-dependent total tension. The fixed-tension-sum exercise states its extra constraint explicitly.

Notation is local when the physical model changes

Some standard letters serve different purposes in different chapters. The setup boxes define them locally; this register makes the collisions explicit. E is Young’s modulus only in the bar-extension discussion, while E elsewhere can name a joint. A is a cross-sectional area only in that same extension formula. C is a compression magnitude in trusses and toggles, a couple in the beam jump derivation, or a named joint when used as a point label. The beam-load gradient k has units of force per length squared; the belt ratio k is dimensionless. The catenary scale a is a length, while the beam point-load coordinate a is another locally defined length. The letter q denotes weight per cable length in Lecture 22, whereas qA, qB, qC in Lecture 12 denote force divided by bar length.

How to distinguish a law, a definition, and a derived result

Newtonian equilibrium is the governing physical premise here. The definitions of internal force, sign convention, or hyperbolic functions establish notation. Coulomb’s friction bound is an assumed empirical contact law. The two-force theorem, cable curves, capstan ratio, and force-reduction formulas are derived consequences of those premises. A proof box establishes a consequence within its assumptions; it does not verify the assumptions for an unspecified real structure.
